speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CONTINUATION OF FLOOR PRICE
speechtext:
Before motions are proceeded with, Mr. Speaker, I desire to make a statement concerning the floor price on beef cattle. I am pleased to be able to inform the house that the floor price for cattle now in effect will continue without change until at least September 1. Hon. members will recall that when the floor price was announced on April 9, the price of 25 cents a pound for good steers, basis delivery at Toronto and Montreal, was to continue in effect until July 1. It was indicated also that the price would be reviewed before June 1, and a further announcement would be made to be effective during July. It was suggested at that time that the matter would be again reconsidered from month to month. I am now suggesting that it will not be reconsidered until September 1, and that the floor price will remain on the same basis until that date.
In view of favourable developments in the marketing of cattle and the sale of meat, it has been decided that the price can be made firm until September 1. The developments to which I refer are, first, that cattle marketings are running at about 25 per cent below the level of last year to the same date. This indicates that farmers are co-operating fully by withholding from market cattle which might normally have been offered for sale; secondly, under the beef exchange agreement with Great Britain and New Zealand it now appears that we can deliver substantially nore beef than was first expected. This is due
[Mr. St. Laurent.l
to the fact that New Zealand, after reviewing their prospective cattle marketings for the balance of the season, have indicated that the quantity of beef available for diversion might approximate 80 million pounds as compared with the original estimate of around 50 million. Eighty million pounds of beef is equal to about 160,000 cattle of average weights as marketed in Canada.
I might add that beef already purchased or offered by the trade amounts to nearly 18 million pounds. Shipping space has been booked and other arrangements made for the orderly delivery of this beef to Great Britain. While no actual deliveries of New Zealand meat have yet been made to United States markets, diversions have been ordered and it is expected that deliveries will be made within the next few weeks.
Another development of fundamental importance is that it is now nearly four weeks since the last known cases of foot-and-mouth disease were dealt with by slaughter and burial. It is expected that by the end of this week all 42 premises on which infected or incontact animals had been slaughtered will have been disinfected for a second time. The placing of test animals on a number of the premises will begin next week. The test animals will be confined on the premises for a period of sixty days, during which they will be kept under close observation and the premises will, of course, be kept under close quarantine. The fact that the disinfection and testing procedures have reached this stage gives reasonable ground for the belief that the disease is under control.
I think I should add that the control procedures have been under continuous observation by veterinarians of the United States department of agriculture, and that we have every reason to believe that the United States authorities regard the work as having been done effectively.
May I conclude this statement by expressing a word of appreciation to the farmers and marketing agencies of the country who have co-operated so fully in regulating the flow of cattle to market. With a continuance of this co-operation, of which we undoubtedly can be assured, I am confident that floor prices can be maintained and that the cattle industry can look forward with confidence.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs? What is Canada's stand with respect to the UNESCO treaty, which came into operation just a few days ago, concerning the removal of tariffs from books and similar items? Can the minister say whether we have signed the treaty? If not, why not?

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Secretary of Slate for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: IMPORTATION OF EDUCATIONAL, SCIENTIFIC AND CULTURAL MATERIALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman was good enough to give me notice of this question, the answer to which is that we have not signed the treaty.
I might say that while the Canadian government is in sympathy with measures to promote and facilitate the international movement of educational, scientific and cultural materials, it has not been possible for Canadian representatives to agree with the

Supply-Defence Production particular proposals embodied in this UNESCO agreement. This treaty or agreement unfortunately does not bind its signatories to remove protective restrictions embodied in their copyright laws or in their quantitative import controls. It would bind countries to abolish their tariffs, which in most cases are not the real obstacles to trade in these matters, while leaving the real obstacles untouched. Many of these educational, scientific and cultural items, I understand, already enter Canada free of duty, and the Canadian tariffs on the remainder are quite modest.
It is felt that it would be difficult to justify the complete removal of our tariffs at a time when other countries were retaining their own special forms of protection which would not have been touched by this treaty.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Defence Production):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when introducing the estimates of the Department of Defence Production a year ago, I indicated that we were embarking on a three-year defence production program, and at that time I outlined in considerable detail the main segments of the program. Again in October, in this chamber, I made a fairly lengthy statement, and on March 31 tabled a report of the Department of Defence Production, covering the period April 1 to December 31, 1951. This report has been available to all hon. members for some time. In addition, a special committee on defence expenditures has been given a great mass of detail concerning defence procurement. In consequence, it is not my intention to describe once again the details of the program.
During the fiscal year 1952-53, present plans contemplate the expenditure by this department of $1,400 million of the moneys voted by parliament for the defence program. Last year at this time our estimated expenditure was some $1,100 million but, as you know, actual expenditures fell short of the estimate by about $200 million, owing largely to developmental and production problems at home and to delays in delivery of military items from abroad.

Our difficulties last year arose through delays in delivery of machine tools, and particularly to delay in securing drawings and specifications from the United States, especially those involving classified projects. Many of these problems have now been overcome to a large extent.
During the last fiscal year, our machine tool division placed orders for more than $31 million worth of machine tools. While this was a definite bottleneck last year, the situation today is materially improved. A substantial number of deliveries have been made and delivery schedules on outstanding orders are, for the most part, satisfactory. We have also secured most of the information necessary to enable us to decide whether we should undertake production in Canada of military items, or whether these should be procured from the United States or abroad.
With regard to security problems, particularly those related to the exchange of classified material, this country has recently signed a security agreement with the United States, under which we take responsibility for security measures in connection with classified U.S. orders placed in this country, and the U.S. government agrees to accept the same responsibility in that country. The agreement contains terms which facilitate the movement of classified material across the border, and enables manufacturers in either country to visit classified establishments in the other country.
Whereas 1951-52 was a period of preparation and organization, 1952-53 will produce actual deliveries and completed facilities.
Without going into details, I might refer briefly to our major production programs. First is aircraft, and the production of two types of jet fighter aircraft constitutes the major projects in this program. Current production of the F-86E at Canadair is twice the rate originally planned, and it is expected to be doubled again by the end of the year. As was announced, we have been able to make some of these aircraft available to the United States out of this year's production, and it is anticipated that further sales will be made out of next year's output. F-86E's will also be made available to the United Kingdom as part of our mutual aid program.
At A. V. Roe it has been necessary to completely design a new fighter aircraft and jet engine-something never previously undertaken in Canada-before production could begin. There has been a great deal of uninformed comment regarding this program, and I should like to put a few facts on the

record. First, let me say that we did not undertake the development of a new type plane and engine just to prove how clever we were or in a spirit of national pride. In general, I am quite satisfied to let others take on the headaches of developmental work in the aircraft field, while we specialize in the production of proven types.
In this case, however, there was no plane in existence that would, in the estimate of competent military authorities, be suitable as an all-weather fighter that could be used in the defence of northern Canada. The only alternative was to produce one in this country. This we undertook to do, and so far the record is reasonably satisfactory. I do not say that we have not had setbacks and delays; we have. However, in comparison to similar programs in other countries, we have made good progress.
For example, the complete design, development, and manufacture of the first CF-100 prototype was accomplished over a period of three years and four months, which was less by several months than the elapsed time to date of the first prototype test flight of the Hawker P.1067, or the Gloster GA-5, both of which are military-type aircraft produced by firms whose development facilities and experience greatly exceed those of A. V. Roe, Canada, Limited. Furthermore, the time required to produce and fly the first production model of the CF-100 compared very favourably with other aircraft of similar type.
Similarly, in the case of the Orenda engine, the two years and six months required from commencement of design to the first test-run was one month less than required for the Rolls-Royce Avon engine, and only a few months longer than required for development of the Sapphire by Armstrong Siddeley.
It is interesting to note just how much has been done in the A.V. Roe plant in the last three years. The following are some of the
facts:
A.V. Roe completed the design and development of the CF-100 fighter between October 1946 and January 1950, a period of slightly over three years. They produced two prototype CF-100 fighter aircraft using United Kingdom Avon engines, and then developed the aircraft using Canadian Orenda engines. They produced one aircraft set of components for test purposes at national research council. In addition, they have developed a plastic canopy for high altitude operation and a satisfactory radome, which is a precision formed plastic nose for radar installation.
As far as the CF-100 aircraft is concerned, tlje company delivered the first pre-production aircraft in June 1951, which is now used by
Supply-Defence Production the company for continued testing and development. The second pre-production aircraft was delivered in October 1951. It was returned for modification owing to structural defect in the wing, but this has now been corrected. Two pre-production aircraft have been delivered to the R.C.A.F. and are now in use for training purposes. Three additional preproduction aircraft have been completed and are now in flight test by the company. Three more aircraft are completely assembled on the final assembly line, in process of equipment installation. The tenth pre-production aircraft is complete structurally and has been transferred to experimental shops for trial installation of certain airborne equipment.
Deliveries of the CF-100 under the main production contract are scheduled to commence in August, 1952. For security reasons, it would be inappropriate to review our planned rate of production, but I have every reason to believe that A.V. Roe will live up to our agreed production schedule, as long as certain electronic equipment can be secured from the United States.
The picture on the Orenda engine is even better. A.V. Roe completed design and development of the TR-5 Orenda engine between April, 1947 and March, 1950, a period slightly less than three years, including complete design and development of the smaller version of the Orenda which is used for test purposes.
They have produced twenty development engines, and ten sets of spare parts for development engines and have completed the 150-hour official type test on the Orenda engine in record time.
They have completed twelve pre-production engines for use in the CF-100 aircraft, and twenty-five sets of spare parts for these engines.
Sixteen Orenda engines on the main production contracts have been produced, and a further thirty-five engine sets completed and in process of assembly.
These few comments may serve to provide hon. members with some measure of the job that has been done by A. V. Roe. It is true that they have not fulfilled every optimistic forecast, but I am satisfied that a good job has been done and that within a few months they will be producing in excess of the schedules established earlier this year.
The other projects at Canadair, de Havil-land, and Canadian Car and Foundry, are all progressing according to plan. As you know, a substantial portion of our aircraft program involves production for United States account. I have just had word that it is the intention of the United States:

Supply-Defence Production government to place another contract in Canada for a new type of trainer aircraft.
How much will that involve?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I would not like to give the amount; the contract is not signed yet.
The shipbuilding program, as presently outlined for the three-year period, amounts to approximately a quarter of a billion dollars. The major project in the program is the construction of 14 destroyer escort vessels, which are primarily of Canadian design and will be almost entirely Canadian made. The propulsion machinery and some of the associated output going into these vessels is being made in Canada for the first time, adding considerably to industrial know-how, as well as to manufacturing facilities in this country. Another major part of the program is the 14 minesweepers now under construction for the Canadian navy which are among the most modern in design for this type of vessel. Three have been launched to date and an additional four will be launched within the next three months. The remaining vessels are expected to be off the ways by the end of the year.
The gun program has an estimated three-year value of approximately $130 million, and of this about $90 million will probably be placed with Canadian manufacturers. The major gun project is the production of the 3" 50 calibre naval gun at Sorel Industries. Deliveries will begin next month.
The first prototype gun has already been through its tests in Canada and has been delivered to the United States navy. It may interest hon. members if I read a wire sent by Admiral Schoeffel, of the United States navy, to the president of Sorel Industries Limited. I quote:
Congratulations on successful completion of first mount. I went to the gun factory to see Sorel's first 3-inch 50 twin gun mount upon completion of its initial inspection there. Admiral Hannon, superintendent of the naval gun factory, met me with a broad smile on his face and said: "This set a record. It is the first gun mount manufactured outside of this factory that has ever in our history passed all inspection with flying colours on its very first submission.'' I extend my most hearty congratulations to United States navy inspection personnel and to the personnel of Sorel for this outstanding achievement in the production of a very complex and difficult item of ordnance. The naval gun factory personnel were loud in their praises of workmanship.
The plant of Sorel Industries, at Sorel, and the Longueuil plant operated by this company, will be the major contractors for all artillery produced in Canada, in order that the department may make full use of the highly-trained staff of gun experts that have been assembled in these two plants. In addition to the 3" 50 calibre naval gun, the program for these plants will include the 105 mm. and 155 mm.
[Mr. Howe.l

Supply-Defence Production because of the ready co-operation of Canadian industry and the flexibility of our industrial structure in this country. Wherever formal orders have been issued, end-use restrictions have been sparingly used. In all but a very small minority of cases, informal consultation between industry and government has been sufficient to get the job done in a satisfactory manner, without saddling the country with an intricate and extensive control apparatus.
During some months of the past year certain strategic materials have been in very tight supply. Probably the most serious of these has been stee1, particularly plate, heavy structural, stainless steel, and seamless tubes. Although our own steel industry has been producing at capacity, and we have been able to import some 750,000 tons of steel more than in the preceding year, it has not been possible to supply all our demands. Many less essential projects have had to be deferred. But I think it is accurate to say that very few direct defence projects have been delayed significantly for reasons connected solely with a shortage of materials. This can properly be considered a measure of the effectiveness of our policies in this regard.
Apart, however, from the most efficient use of the available materials, it is heartening to note the solid progress that has been made during the last twelve months in the development of additional capacity to produce strategic materials. In previous statements in the house-when I last spoke on this department's estimates-I mentioned the expansion that was then getting under way in the steel industry. This expansion has gone forward with all possible co-operation from the government, and is continuing today. Some parts of this program have been completed and when the other parts are completed this year and next, a most important addition will have been made to the country's industrial base. Our primary capacity will then be greater than it was in 1950 by about one-third and a wider variety of products will be turned out by the industry than formerly.
In Quebec and Labrador the work preparatory to the production of iron ore, including construction of a 350-mile railway line from Seven Islands to Burnt Creek, has been speeded up. It now seems possible that delivery of ore will begin sooner than was originally expected, perhaps as early as 1954.
The defence requirements for nickel have resulted in a serious shortage of that metal. Our two major suppliers, International Nickel Company of Canada, Limited, and Falcon-bridge Nickel Mines, Limited, have been expanding their production. Sherritt-Gordon Mines, Limited, are making rapid progress in opening up their Lynn Lake deposits, and 
initial production from the new property is expected early in 1954. These developments will result in a substantial increase in the supply of this essential metal for the free world.
The mill at the Emerald tungsten mine, to which I referred last year, has been put in operation and is now producing substantial amounts of tungsten concentrates. Similarly, our incentive price schedule for cobalt has resulted in a 50 per cent increase in the available supplies of this essential metal.
The vast undertaking of the Aluminum Company of Canada in British Columbia scarcely needs emphasis. Furthermore, this company is making very substantial additions to its capacity to produce aluminum in Quebec. As Canadian production of aluminum is far greater than the amount we use, it is worth noting that this economic producer will be in a position to continue to meet competition anywhere in the world.
The exploration and development of our petroleum resources in western Canada goes on at a rising rate. Already more than one-third of Canada's domestic requirements of petroleum and petroleum products are being met from supplies produced in this country. If the discovery of oil and gas continues at the present rate, Canada should be able to produce the equivalent of its own requirements of these materials within the next decade.
The expansion of our chemicals industry has been very rapid. The world shortage of sulphur has required some limitation of our normal requirements, but a number of projects to relieve this shortage have been undertaken. The Shell Oil Company has completed a small plant at Jumping Pound,. Alberta, to recover elemental sulphur from natural gas and the Royalite Oil Company has-a similar plant scheduled to be completed very shortly. At Copper Cliff a plant to-recover sulphur dioxide gas for use in the paper industry will be completed later this-year and several paper companies are installing equipment to roast our native pyrites rather than rely on imported sulphur. Additional sulphuric acid capacity has been, installed to use Canadian pyrite or other sulphides as the source of sulphur for the basic chemical.
Apart from the plants built to relieve the sulphur shortage, Canada has witnessed a very great expansion in its other chemical operations. Some $200 million is being invested in new plants to make petrochemicals nylon intermediates, plastic components for structural and insulation purposes, chlorine and caustic soda and a wide range of other basic chemicals. Many of these plants will produce chemicals not.

hitherto made in Canada, but which are needed in our expanding industrial development.
I have referred to the current easing in pressure upon the supply of some strategic materials. This is occurring not only in Canada but also in the United States and in other countries of the free world. Thus, whatever action it is thought feasible to take in Canada, by way of relaxing our present controls, must take into account what is done elsewhere. It is necessary, for example, to give due consideration to the recommendations of the international materials conference on materials which are still under allocation by that body. And the degree and rate of decontrol in the United States likewise bears upon our decisions in Canada.
I scarcely need say that the government, like industry, would welcome a return to conditions where the supply of materials is such that normal commercial channels would provide satisfactory distribution. For some materials this is now possible.
Just a few days ago non-ferrous metals orders 6, 7 and 8 were revoked eliminating all controls on zinc, cadmium and antimony. The situation regarding other materials will be watched very carefully and remaining controls will be relaxed or removed as rapidly as it appears advisable.
In closing I would like to repeat that we are now entering another phase of the defence production program. Industry now has a pretty clear idea of the general outline of the program. We have passed through the major part of the development and tooling-up stage, and this year will mark the first year of volume production with deliveries coming forward at an increasing rate. I would also like to remind the house once again that this program has a large element of insurance in it. At the same time that we are producing the weapons and equipment needed to maintain a modern army we are further expanding our industrial strength. On both counts, I am satisfied we will meet our objectives.

Mr. Chairman, the statement just made by the Minister of Defence Production will require a great deal of study and I would not presume to attempt today to deal with all the details he has furnished the committee. However, we on this side of the house have several subjects to place before him and the committee with regard to the work of this department and we would ask the minister to let us have his comments on these different questions.
The amount of money sought by the department for this fiscal year amounts to something over $98 million, but in addition the minister
Supply-Defence Production and his department will be spending approximately $1,400 million for the Department of National Defence, as he explained in opening his remarks today. That portion of the defence department estimates is about two-thirds of their total vote and is about one-third of the total moneys for all departments voted for the present fiscal year. So this Department of Defence Production is by far the most important spending department of the government. For that reason, as well as the importance of the estimates now being considered, these matters should mean a great deal to the committee and to the country.
I regret that the details given in the estimates are so scanty as to make it most difficult to get much of a picture of what is being done by this department. I hope that in another year it will be possible to have more details given. We had a very good report from the department covering the period from its inception on April 1, 1951, until the end of that year. But I do hope that in future years we shall have greater details and that the estimates of the department will be broken down into further subheadings.
The first comment I wish to make today with regard to the work of the department is that the minister seems to be placing much of his emphasis on the fact that this is a three-year plan. I think he called it a three-year defence production program. That program started well over a year ago so that we are now in the second year and the plan is almost half completed. I believe that the world situation today is such that it calls for a degree of permanence with respect to the functions of the Department of Defence Production, but there does not seem to have been much consideration given to the longterm work of the department. Mind you, there may not be a long period of tension, but the only thing that will prevent it is a third world war or a great change in the attitude of the communists.
The whole plan of the freedom loving nations is 'based on becoming so strong and remaining so strong that the communists dare not start a third world war. I believe that the Department of Defence Production should make its plans accordingly. Yet in the speech of the minister today and in the published report of the department all the emphasis has been placed on the three-year program. I point out, for example, that on page 156 of the estimates we find that this department has 75 officials who are described as officers on loan from business and industry, and for whom salary provision is not required. The different positions are listed which they hold. I take it that most of these positions are very important ones
2748	HOUSE OF
Supply-Defence Production in the Department of Defence Production. I am not quarrelling with that situation, at the moment, but there seems to be a clear indication that the department is working on an emergency basis and is taking men from industry for a short period of time and not paying them a salary because their salaries are paid by their firms. It seems to be an emergency operation, a short-term plan.
When the three-year period has expired, even if the department is able to complete its program there will still be need for a great deal of work to be done by the department. I notice that on page 9 of the annual report their main responsibilities are summarized as procurement of all requirements of the Department of National Defence, and second, the responsibility for taking whatever steps are necessary to ensure an adequate supply of materials to support the defence procurement program. That work will carry on indefinitely, certainly as long as we are living in this present state of tension. When the minister replies I would ask him to give us some idea of the plans of his department for the period at the end of the three-year program which, as I said, is less than two years from the present time. That is the first subject on which I would ask him to comment.
My second suggestion is that the time has now come to look again at the extreme powers given to the department last year when the Defence Production Act first became law. I refer particularly to the power which is described in the United States as the seizure power. As hon. members know, there have been great arguments in the United States within the last few weeks concerning President Truman's action in seizing the steel industry, apparently relying on his powers as the chief executive officer of that great nation. The question as to whether or not he had the right to do so is now before the supreme court of the United States, and until it is settled no one can say whether or not the President had the right to take that drastic action.
I do not doubt for a minute that most Canadians have been patting themselves on the back, if that were physically possible, and saying: The Americans may have troubles like that but it could not happen in Canada. Actually under the Defence Production Act it could happen in Canada, and there could not be any question about the legality of a seizure of that type simply because of the terms of the act. I would refer you, Mr. Chairman, to section 27 of the Defence Production Act passed about a year ago, which reads as follows:
(1) Where the minister is satisfied that
(a)	a person who has entered into a defence contract has failed! or is likely to fail-


Those are pretty far-reaching words; they could not be much more so.
-to perform the contract in a businesslike and efficient manner,
(b)	a person who has entered into a defence contract has failed to keep proper and detailed accounts and records of the cost of the work performed under the contract, or
(c)	a person to whom a direction has been given under section 23-
Section 23 enables the minister to order' a person to comply with a contract.
-or who is required pursuant to a regulation to give priority in the carrying on of his business to the production of or dealing in defence supplies, or construction of defence projects has failed without reasonable excuse to comply with the direction or regulation or the minister is satisfied that he will so fail or is likely so to fail-
Again these are terribly wide powers.
-the minister may authorize another person (in this act called a "controller") to carry on, until the minister otherwise directs, the whole or any part of the business of that person.
(2) Where a controller has been appointed to carry on a business or a part thereof, he shall be deemed to be the agent of the owner thereof for the purpose of carrying on the business or that part thereof, except that the owner shall not have any right to control the business or that part thereof and the controller may-
"The owner shall not have any right", mind you.
-subject to any instructions of the minister, do all such things as he thinks fit for the purpose of carrying on the business or that part thereof.
Then, the third subsection gives the power to compel industry to furnish whatever information is required by the controller. Not only does the minister have this drastic seizure power, but he can assign that right to one of his officials. In section 5 of the Defence Production Act, we find these words under the sidenote, "Minister's authority to assign powers":
The minister may authorize any person, on his behalf and under his control and direction, to do any act or thing or to exercise any power that the minister may do or exercise under this act.
Today we are legally in the position that the minister or anyone he chooses to authorize can seize practically any industry in Canada- certainly, he could seize the steel industry. That power was clearly a wartime power. We brought that point up during the debate last year, and the Prime Minister admitted that it was a war power. I would refer members to page 908 of Hansard for March 5, 1951, where I asked this question of the Prime Minister:
Then may I ask the Prime Minister whether any further powers would be required to carry out defence production if we were actually in a third world war?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I do not anticipate there would be.
He made a statement to the same effect on the following page. We also find that

clearly set out in the report of the department, which we received a short time ago, at page 14:
Although the powers now in effect are virtually the same as those which existed during the last war, it has been understood that these powers would be used to the minimum extent necessary.
The minister admitted a year ago that he had had the co-operation of industry up to that date. On the same page of Hansard I asked him this question:
But has there been any difficulty that would require the taking over of a business, for example?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Not yet, no.
Nothing of that kind?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
No.
Today the minister has said that he has been getting ready co-operation from the business world of Canada. He has said also that the general situation is much better, that materials are in much better supply. He said that we had now entered a new phase in this defence production program. He intimates everything is going along very well. I do suggest in all earnestness that the time has now come to give up that seizure power. I believe that it has not been necessary at all. I do not believe that such a power should ever have been taken in peacetime. I think it is unfair to the Canadian people to continue that power on the statute books of Canada. There would be plenty of other powers left in the Defence Production Act to enable the minister and his officials to carry on their program without any difficulty.
The third subject on which I would ask a comment from the minister is this. Has the time not come to consider the distribution of Canadian defence orders by countries? I do not intend to deal with the distribution of defence orders in the different parts of Canada; that will be brought up by other members of our party. I am referring to the orders to be placed outside of Canada. At page 51 of the department report we find what is called "Appendix G", and it is entitled, "Distribution of Canadian defence orders by countries, from April 1 to December 31, 1951." This list shows that there was a total of $1,431,000,000 worth of orders placed during the period. Broken down into areas, you have $987,500,000-I am only giving the round figures-worth of orders placed within Canada. Orders to almost half of that value, namely $412,600,000 were placed in the United States, and only $31,400,000 were placed in other countries. A very small proportion of these orders which went beyond the orders of Canada were placed in any country other than the United States.
We all know that there have been large purchases of defence material from our neighbouring country. We know also that it has
Supply-Defence Production been pretty much a one-way street. When we were first told about this program we were led to expect that large United States orders would be placed in Canada. I do not know what the figures are at the present time, but certainly up until this year the amount of defence equipment ordered by the United States has been very small compared with the moneys Canada has expended for defence equipment in the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Would the hon. member like the figure?
Yes, I should like the minister to give the figure later.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: You said it was very small, and perhaps I should correct that. It stands today at $195 million.
For what period?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That is to date.
From what time would that run?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Almost from the beginning of the defence program.
Is that from April 1, 1951, or from what date?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: From July 1, 1951, to date.
That is equal to a little over half of the orders we have placed in the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: More than that and United States orders are coming in very fast.

There would be great benefit to Canada if as many of these products as possible could be purchased from the United Kingdom rather than from the United States. This is not the place to go into the details on that, but I would point out that in British Columbia we are extremely worried about selling our canned salmon, our lumber and our apples. The only reason we cannot sell them to the United Kingdom is because of the exchange situation. If Canada bought more war equipment in the United Kingdom, she would sell that much more of her own products. I do not think that could be questioned. I repeat that the time has come to consider again this question of the distribution of defence orders which go outside of our country.
Then it would seem that it would be wise also to review again this policy of a widespread standardization with the United States in the use of military equipment. We have that referred to throughout the report of the department. For example, at page 22 we find: As a result of the government's decision to adopt United States-type of army equipment, this division, in order to meet the most urgent requirements.

Supply-Defence Production negotiated with United States authorities for the purchase of initial supplies of many types of ammunition.
Then at page 23:
The decision to standardize on United States army equipment on most items necessitated early decisions regarding types of weapons that could efficiently be produced in Canada.
It has not worked out just as well as had been expected. A little further down on the same pages we find paragraphs which give some idea of the difficulties. For example, on page 22 there is this paragraph:
Because of the failure to agree on standardization of small arms, there was little production of smaller calibre ammunition, although some export orders were received for the types previously produced in Canada.
And at page 23:
Contracts placed for small arms have been limited, due to failure to achieve international agreement on standardization for these types of equipments. However, orders have been placed in Canada for -50 Browning machine guns and small quantities of -22 rifles and survival weapons.
Then we find another result on page 25 of the report where there is mention of tanks. We find this paragraph:
Tanks had been ordered from the United States, but in November action on these orders was suspended, and a contract demand was received for the purchase of Centurion tanks from the United Kingdom.
That is a good illustration of the point I am placing before the minister. The government set out to get United States tanks. Then they could not get them, or it was found that they were not as good as Centurion tanks produced in the United Kingdom. Now we are to get tanks from Great Britain.
Canadian troops serving in Korea are serving in the commonwealth division and Canadian troops in Germany are serving with or are attached to the troops of the United Kingdom. I believe that the government has been making a fetish of equipping Canadians with United States equipment, and that that decision should be reviewed without further delay.
Among the orders placed in the United States last year we find $68 million for United States-type equipment for two infantry divisions. We sent our British equipment for three divisions overseas to the other NATO countries. Now we are starting to buy from the United States equipment for two divisions. We seem to be in the position that we do not know what sort of rifle our troops are going to use if there is another war. The British, of course, are planning to use the [DOT]280 and the Americans the Garand. Canada sits in between; and unless the situation has changed recently, is not making any rifles.
[Mr. Green.1
It is not known just what our troops are to use. That is a bad situation and it should be dealt with without delay.
Then there are two other questions to which I wish to direct attention. One is with regard to the shipbuilding program. Today the minister pointed to the war vessels we are building or which are being ordered. A statement will be found at page 25 of the report. It is stated there-and the minister confirmed it today-that there are to be fourteen escort vessels. What are they going to escort? I suggest to the committee that they will be escorting Canadian freighters or possibly freighters of other nations. Yet Canada is still in the position that she has nothing but old, slow cargo vessels built during the last war. We have not gone ahead with our plans for building modem vessels which themselves might be able to get away from submarines or which certainly would need far less protection than these old slow boats.
I think that building escort vessels is only building up the wall on one side. Do not forget that the merchant navy is a part of our forces, if a war comes. It is the fourth arm of the services. I am afraid that we are going to find ourselves with some nice, new, fast escort vessels and nothing but these old, slow cargo freighters which, as I said a week or two ago, are nothing more or less than sitting ducks for the fast Russian submarines. I suggest to the minister that a start be made now on modernizing Canada's merchant navy. That is really just as much a part of the defence plan as are all these other undertakings.
Then finally, I wish to mention one other subject on which the minister and I have had words on other days, and it is this. I should like to know what steps, if any, are being taken or are in contemplation to assist in the establishment of a steel industry in Canada west of the great lakes. At the present time there is no steel industry in that part of Canada other than perhaps small plants which can turn scrap metal into steel. At page 36 of the report I find this paragraph dealing with iron and steel:
The division-
The materials branch of the department. -has, where necessary, assisted Canadian iron and steel producers in obtaining essential materials and equipment in Canada or elsewhere for the maintenance or expansion of their facilities. Progress was made towards the expansion of Canada's basic iron and steel facilities during 1951.
I pointed out to the minister some months ago that iron ore was being shipped from British Columbia to Japan, and that we were buying back the steel at a tremendously

increased cost. We find that this practice is still going on. I have here a dispatch from the Vancouver press of May 5, just a few weeks ago, which sets out that they will be shipping 100,000 tons a month of iron ore from Quinsam on Vancouver island and Iron River and 30,000 tons a month from Texada island. There appears to be no plan under way by the department for getting a steel industry established in that part of Canada.
I was also surprised to read a report of a speech made by the Minister of Transport with regard to the use of the iron ore in Quebec and Labrador. The Minister of Defence Production said today that he expected that iron ore would be coming from those vast deposits by 1954; but he did not say anything about the use of that iron ore for further expansion of Canada's steel industry. On May 8 the Minister of Transport was reported as saying at Quebec:
The federal government is keeping in mind the possibility of an expanded Canadian steel industry through use of Quebec-Labrador iron ore, transport minister Chevrier said tonight.
However, he said it is still too early to make any positive prediction on the subject.
That appears to indicate that there is in the minds of the cabinet no plan to drive ahead for a greatly expanded Canadian steel industry using this iron ore deposit. I regret that. I hope there is actually some plan being worked out, because I believe that steel will always be the key to the future greatness of this nation. The minister says we are still very short and are going to be so short this year that many projects will have to be deferred. I hope he can give us some assurance on this point as well when he replies to the various subjects that have been raised this afternoon.
Those are all the points I wish to place before him at the moment. When we get into the general questioning, no doubt other matters will come up for consideration.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
As the hon. member for Van-couver-Quadra has already pointed out there is a very close relationship between the estimates now before us, the estimates of the Department of Defence Production, and the estimates of the Department of National Defence.
Earlier this afternoon the Minister of Defence Production indicated that in addition to the sum of close to $100 million being asked for directly for the Department of Defence Production, his department is also handling the spending of $1,400 million in connection with the procurement of equipment for the Department of National Defence. That means that before us this afternoon we
Supply-Defence Production really have just about one-fifteenth of the expenditures in which the Minister of Defence Production has a hand.
With respect to that other huge sum, $1,400 million, we will of course have an opportunity to discuss it when we are on the estimates of the Department of National Defence, and also when the committee on defence expenditure makes its report back to the house. Nevertheless, I hope that during the course of these estimates we may get a little more explanation from the Minister of Defence Production as to the part that he or his department plays in the estimates of the Department of National Defence. I should like to know whether the Minister of Defence Production merely places the orders, merely plays the role of a delivery boy, although I find it hard to think of him in those terms. Does he just place the orders that are handed to him by the Department of National Defence, or does he personally examine the proposals of the Department of National Defence, and have something to say about the whole defence program?
The estimates that are before us relate to the setting up of plant and equipment, but we would be interested in knowing what part the minister plays in that other aspect of our defence expenditures. When the estimates of those two departments are submitted to treasury board, for example, are they submitted independently of each other, or are they submitted together? There are further questions, but they can be asked when we get to the stage where we are asking individual questions.
I should like also if the Minister of Defence Production would bring us up to date as to the picture in relation to the various plants in which public money has been invested. When we get down to one of the items of the estimates of the minister we find a reference to three different categories. First, there is the group known as private plants; then there is the group known as crown plants operating on a management-fee basis, and finally there is the group known as crown companies under the Minister of Defence Production.
We should like to know how much money has been invested in each of those categories of plants since the commencement of the Department of Defence Production; indeed since the commencement of the whole current defence program. We are also interested in the question as to the decentralization, or the lack of it, of industry. Indeed my colleague, the hon. member for Cape Breton South, will have something to say on that during the

Supply-Defence Production course of the discussion this afternoon, and he likewise will have something to say on the steel industry.
Mr. Chairman, I listened with interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Van-couver-Quadra. There were sections of what he had to say with which we are in agreement; but it follows from that, that there are some things that he said with which we do not agree. The only thing that bothers me about what I shall now be saying is that it always gives a bit of comfort to the Minister of Defence Production. He always likes the situation where the Tories are coming at him from one side and we are coming at him from the other. He says: I am all right; I am right in the middle. He should realize, however, that that is sometimes known as sitting on the fence.
At any rate, the hon. member for Van-couver-Quadra complained, in keeping with complaints he and the members of his party have made in the past, against the wide powers enjoyed by the Minister of Defence Production as set out in the act which set up the department. Our complaint against the minister is akin to the comment that we made the other day when we were on the resolution to extend the Emergency Powers Act. Our complaint is that some of the powers which were conferred upon the Minister of Defence Production have not been used. During the discussion of this measure last year it was brought out that the powers conferred upon the Minister of Defence Production included the power to control prices of goods and materials affected by the defence purchasing program.
I think I am stating the case fairly when I make that distinction; for the minister wanted it clear that he was not being given over-all price control powers. But he did admit that he would have the power to control prices where there was inflation, where there was an increase in prices, owing to defence purchasing.
There is no doubt but that the high level of prices, the high cost of living that our people are experiencing at the present time, is to a large extent due to that very factor, namely the very heavy stream of defence purchasing. We feel that the minister should long ago have made use of some of the powers that were conferred upon him by parliament to protect the living standards of the people.
I do not know of any case-there may be one, and if the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra can tell us about it and point it out I would be glad to hear it-where the people of Canada have suffered by the use

or the abuse of the powers that were conferred upon the Minister of Defence Production in this emergency legislation. I do know that the people of Canada have suffered because the powers under that legislation, together with the powers under the Emergency Powers Act, were not used to control prices and to protect the living standards of the Canadian people.
Similarly, I think along different lines from the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra when he expresses his concern over the power given to the Minister of Trade and Commerce to seize certain industries. Here, too, as so often happens, it seems to me that one can do a form of arguing just by the words he picks out. By using the word "seizure" one would seem to be suggesting something sinister and against the interests of the people. But there are times when what has been described as seizure by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra is nothing more or less than the people of a country, through their elected representatives, taking control of something of concern to all the people.
Members generally have no hesitancy in doing that sort of thing at a time of real crisis, such as a time of war. They do not object even to its being done in a time of apprehended war, or a time of defence preparation because of fear of war. But the minute the pressure is off, the minute there is a notion in some quarters that a state of crisis no longer exists, there is this plea that the people's representatives should leave the economy alone.
As a matter of fact in his remarks this afternoon the Minister of Defence Production came pretty close to that for which the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra is asking, because he said he was glad he had not been called upon to use his powers in the way some of us wanted him to use them. And he went on to express the private-enterprise dream and hope that it might be possible soon to get back to the normal way of doing things.
Well, that is our quarrel with both the Minister of Defence Production and his party, and with the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra and his party. They are quite prepared to have government ownership, government operation and direct economic controls when the demands of war are placed upon us, or even the demands of defence production. But they want none of that, except when confronted with that kind of crisis. We contend that the interests of the people of Canada as a whole, in terms of their standard of living, in terms of housing and in terms of social security deserve just

as much attention as do these special problems that arise at times of international crisis.
And so I wished simply to express our views in this matter. I have no doubt but that our position will be misinterpreted. I have no doubt some will say we want centralization and controls, and there will be the misleading use of the word "seizure", the word used this afternoon by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra. We do not advocate any of our ideas for their own sake; we want simply the same measure of economic democracy and the same control of the economy in peacetime that all parties are prepared to practise in wartime. All parties agree that in a time of war and a time of national emergency we have to face up to those situations and deal with them in the best way possible. We feel, further, that in peacetime the problems of housing and social security, together with our health and living standards, are of concern to the people, and that we should deal with them in the same sensible way. namely, the rule of law. In other words, we believe in economic democracy.

Mr. Chairman, I was specially interested in the closing remarks of the minister when, as I understood him, he said that our program of defence production was accomplishing not only its primary purpose, but also a secondary and beneficial one in that it was strengthening the industrial potential of the country. I am not yet convinced that his second statement is entirely true, because I feel that if the economy of our country is to be strengthened up to something approaching its greatest potential, then it must be done in the most beneficial way possible. And, unless conditions have changed over the last few months, I suggest the minister is not justified in making that assertion.
I was interested in a reply to questions asked by the hon. member for Brandon, as it is reported at page 691 of Hansard for November 5, 1951. There were two questions, as follows:
1.	What defence contracts, if any, have been awarded by the Department of Defence Production in each of the prairie provinces, monthly, since July 1, 1951?
2.	What defence contracts have been awarded in Ontario and Quebec, monthly, during the same period?
To those questions the parliamentary assistant replied:
At the last session a question similar in form to this one was asked, and at that time it was pointed out that it is not possible to give accurate figures in answer to this type of question. It was pointed out that lists of the contracts awarded are published each two weeks, and these lists of course are available to any member at any time. There
Supply-Defence Production is this weakness in them, that the address shown of the contractor is merely a mailing address and may or may not give an indication as to where the contract is being carried out.
If that statement means what I assume it means it implies that the Department of Defence Production keeps no check and makes no stipulations with regard to where defence production shall be carried on. It seems to me that that is one of the primary and fundamental requirements for a strong defence effort. After all we are not living in the days of 1914. This is 1952; and if world war III comes it is inevitable that we will be subjected to devastating atomic bombing by our potential enemy. We must live with that fact, and realize that if our defence production is to be effective it should be carried on in a way which will subject it to the least possible dangers in time of war.
In the same connection the hon. member for Moose Jaw, while speaking in the debate on December 3, 1951, is reported in Hansard as having given some interesting figures in connection with defence contracts allotted between April 1 and October 31, 1951. According to his figures -03 per cent-that is, three one-hundredths of one per cent-of all contracts were let in Newfoundland. About one third of one per cent were let in Prince Edward Island; about one third of one per cent in the Yukon and the Northwest Territories; and two per cent in Alberta; while at the same time more than 75 per cent of all contracts were let in Ontario and Quebec combined.
It seems to me that insufficient thought is given to a program which would require that defence production be carried out over a larger area and in a way which would permit two benefits to accrue-(1), the most important, that these industries would be relatively safe from attack in time of war and (2), which in the long run might be the more important of the two, the benefits which would accrue from the development of industries in our smaller centres and in the undeveloped parts of the country, including depressed areas. We have large areas in our country which are not able to absorb the natural increase in population. In that regard I should like to quote from an article with reference to the prairie provinces, as follows:
The prairie provinces have not merely failed to attract population from elsewhere. They are, in fact, losing their own population. Their natural increase (excess of births over deaths) during 194151 was 396,394; but their actual population increase was 115,644, It is clear from this that between 1941 and 1951 they lost 280,750 people-a disaster as great, from the population viewpoint, as if Winnipeg and its suburbs had been wiped off the map.

Supply-Defence Production
The same is true of the situation in the maritime provinces. These are things which should be of vital importance to the government, and especially to several ministers. In addition to the Minister of Defence Production they should be of vital interest to the minister of defence, the minister of health and welfare, and the Minister of Resources and Development. It is not only the sparsely settled and underdeveloped areas which suffer from this program, or perhaps I should say this lack of program; our larger cities also suffer. Population figures show that during the last ten years our large cities have tended to become larger and our small centres have not grown at as rapid a rate. There are whole areas which are experiencing hardly any development at all.
There are a great many disadvantages that stem from this unordered but rapid growth of our large cities. Our country is carrying a load of defence and social welfare costs which is necessary and to have saddled upon it these other unnecessary problems which arise from the rapid and disorganized growth of our large cities simply adds to the burden. These problems are many. There is the problem of communications and transportation. For instance, the city of Toronto has found it necessary to build an underground transportation system which is using up large amounts of concrete and reinforcing steel and things of that sort which could be used for defence purposes elsewhere. That construction would not be necessary if the present transportation system were not overloaded because of the rapidly increasing population. I cite that as an example, but there are many others that could be cited. May I quote from a press digest as follows:
Traffic tie-ups are not unusual in most Canadian cities and downtown parking space is similarly at a premium but New York city outdoes all rivals. The Times says that in the commercial centre-the nine square miles south of Sixtieth street-traffic is "slowing New York to an oxcart pace." The reasons:
Every working day 3,750,000 persons pour into that area.
Into its 270 miles of streets come 380,000 automobiles, trucks and busses.
The same sort of thing is beginning to happen even here in Ottawa. I understand that something like 50,000 motor vehicles have been registered in this area whereas there are parking spaces for only 6,000. These things place unnecessary loads on all municipalities. I maintain that they could be avoided if industry, especially defence industry, were encouraged to make use of the potentials in materials, manpower and transportation available in the smaller centres.
As our larger centres grow rapidly there is a tendency for the central parts to decay and

eventually become slums. In that connection, I should like to quote as follows:
Blighted areas work havoc with the cost side of the balance sheet as well. The disproportionate costs of blighted districts in a representative group of American cities are concisely demonstrated in the following relationships:
Although slums and blighted districts comprise about 20 per cent of the metropolitan residential areas they account for: 33 per cent of the population: 45 per cent of the major crimes; 55 per cent of the juvenile delinquency; 50 per cent of the disease; 45 per cent of the city service costs; 6 per cent of the real estate tax revenues.
That is one of the problems that our municipalities have to face at the present time. This situation is just as true for Canada, as the data available for major cities like Saint John, New Brunswick, Montreal, Ottawa, Toronto, Hamilton, Winnipeg and Vancouver indicate the same underlying conditions.
It has been shown also that our large cities are not healthful places in which to live. It has been shown statistically that tuberculosis is becoming a large-city disease. In 18 cities of the United States with populations of 500,000 or more the average tuberculosis death rate during 1947 to 1949 was 42-9 per 100,000 of population, as compared to only 29-6 per 100,000 of population for the whole country.
I do not wish to labour the point, but I believe it is true that it is not beneficial for our economy as a whole that our large cities should be allowed to get much larger while our smaller places are allowed to decay and not develop. I should like to press upon the government, and especially upon the Minister of Defence Production, since he could do the most about it simply because he probably spends more money than any other minister for production of various types, the evils of allowing our industries to congregate in a few centres.
In addition to what I have said about the problems which arise through large cities growing too rapidly there is the obvious danger from bombing. We must realize that if world war III ever becomes a reality we will be subjected to bombing, probably by atomic bombs which can destroy everything within a radius of half a mile and do great damage in a much greater radius. There are other disadvantages which ensue from allowing our industries to flock together in a few large centres.
For example, it has been estimated that it costs the workers in the A. V. Roe plant in Toronto approximately $12,000 a day merely to get to work. I know of a lot of small centres where a plant of that sort would be appreciated and where the whole

economy of the district could be improved without placing too great a load upon the present available housing and transportation facilities.
To be fair, the government probably has plans in this direction, at least I hope it has. I trust the government realizes the benefits of carrying out a program of dispersing industry over as large an area as possible, over all provinces and into small towns and rural areas, or into entirely new centres if necessary. I do not mean to suggest that existing plants should be uprooted and transferred somewhere else, but new plants should be built for the most part in the smaller communities, and when plants have to be replaced they should be rebuilt in some other area. It may be argued that large cities are necessary, that they are efficient and provide a better standard of living. I should like to quote briefly from a speech delivered by Alfred North Whitehead at Harvard university in 1930. It is published in a Pelican book called "Adventures of Ideas". He said:
Throughout the whole span of civilization up to the present moment, the growth of condensed aggregates of humans, which we call cities, has been an inseparable accompaniment of the growth of civilization. There are many obvious reasons: the defence of accumulated wealth behind city walls, the concentration of power in the form of human muscles and, later, in the form of available heat energy, the ease of mutual intercourse required for business relations, the pleasure from a concentration of aesthetic and cultural opportunities, the advantages of concentration of governmental and other directing agencies, administrative, legal and military. . . But, if we examine the trend of technology during the past generation, the reasons for this concentration are largely disappearing. Still more, the reasons for the choice of sites for cities are also altering. Mechanical power can be transmitted for hundreds of miles, men can communicate almost instantaneously by telephone.
He points out that large modern cities are not necessarily the most efficient areas of production, nor are they areas which produce the highest standard of living for a given income. I see one glimmer of hope in the report of the Department of Defence Production. On page 10 there is the following with reference to the department:
It also includes Defence Construction (1951) Limited, a crown company responsible for the construction of barracks, radar stations, and other defence projects, and a small industries division which seeks to ensure that all segments of Canadian industry are given an opportunity to make their appropriate contributions to the defence production program.
I hope that phase of the efforts of the Department of Defence Production will be pressed forward as strongly as possible, and that the maximum benefits accruing from such a program will be realized. There are a few things on which I should like to have some information from the minister. First of
Supply-Defence Production all, I am concerned with the problem of the mechanics of safeguarding our system of carrying on the work of what would be very important departments if a world war should suddenly start. What would be our position in the case of a Pearl Harbor type of attack on us? Is there any safeguarding of government files? Are there duplicate files somewhere else so that business could carry on the next day even if an atomic bomb were dropped somewhere in the minister's department tonight?
Hon. members are laughing, but if our defence production means anything its purpose is to prevent a third world war, and we may not be able to prevent it. If we are thinking of realities at all we must anticipate such an event and recognize that it is useless to build up a vast organization which can be destroyed overnight. It might be suggested of course that if an atomic bomb were dropped on Ottawa tonight business could not be carried on anyway because no doubt parliament would be destroyed. If we were lucky enough to have the bomb dropped on a Friday night I think a large number of members would escape the tragedy.
Some hon. members may take the attitude that there is not much that can be done about this situation. After all, how do you go about pushing industries around or telling them they cannot locate in one place and should locate somewhere else? Other countries have recognized this problem long ago. As is generally known, in Great Britain a royal commission was established to consider the distribution of industrial population, and out of its work came legislation such as the special areas act, the distribution of industry act and the town and country planning act, all of which are designed to develop the country evenly, to disperse its industry so it will be less vulnerable to attack and to increase employment in depressed areas.
For instance, in the case of the distribution of industry act, the introduction reads as follows:
An act to provide for the development of certain areas; for controlling the provision of industrial premises with a view to securing the proper distribution of industry; and for purposes connected with the matters aforesaid.
The United States has also realized that if their economy is to be helped and if the fabric of their production system is to be strong their industry must be dispersed and must have its roots in the small towns and hamlets as well as in the large cities. They recognize that if another war comes the large cities will be primary targets. Realizing that, the United States has already taken some action in this regard. I should like

Supply-Defence Production to read a news item reported in the U.S. News and World Report of August 13, 1948. It reads as follows:
A guide is being offered' to owners of industry who want to be as secure as possible in the event of future war. This guide calls for dispersal of plants in time of peace so as to be prepared for war.
Official advice to businessmen on how best to meet the threat of world war III is given by the national security resources board. This board, headed by Arthur M. Hill, is charged with planning to co-ordinate military, industrial and civilian defence. Its advice, given in a report just made, is this:
Decentralization should be seriously considered by industry in its long-range planning, with a shift of new plants away from centres of industry. Small towns offer the best opportunity for industries seeking safety in the event of war. Plants in these areas are least likely to be the object of bombing attacks.
On the subject of attack it has this to say:
Attack, when it comes, will aim at a few key industrial centres. Warning may not be given. No location in U.S. will be out of range of enemy bombers or enemy sabotage. Destructive effects may be many times those of Pearl Harbor. Attempt will be made to knock out key war industry with the first surprise blow. Atomic bombs probably will be used. Those bombs, in the past, have been able to destroy nearly everything within a radius of half a mile from their centre of detonation. They have caused moderate damage to all structures within another 1\ miles of that area. Allowing for future developments, the atom bomb is not expected to cause heavy damage beyond a distance of three miles from its point of detonation. Area destroyed by each bomb, thus, will be small. Number of bombs used will be relatively small. They are highly difficult to make, will remain very expensive. Being scarce, they must be used on concentrated targets of great strategic importance. An enemy in tne foreseeable future, thus, cannot bomb every big factory, even every big city.
That lends point to the argument that our industry should be dispersed so that each factory producing war material would be in a different location. Then any potential enemy could not possibly have enough atomic bombs to destroy them all.
Summing up, this board recommends the following principles with regard to industry in the United States, so that its potential war industry may be as strong as possible if world war III should occur. The accompanying chart is headed "Where to build factories in the atomic age." It says:
Safest sites are:
In cities of less than 50,000 people:
At least 10 miles from a major city;
At least 3 miles from any strategic industry;
In industrial areas of not more than 5 square miles;
Away from major air bases, dams, power plants;
In hilly country, rather than in a flat area.
Then, too, the important thing I have already mentioned is the beneficial effects which accrue to small towns and hamlets if they can contribute to the war potential in their own area. The United States has recognized that point. In that connection I

should like to quote briefly from an advertisement appearing on page 2 of Look for April 8, 1952. It says in part:
As a prime contractor for the armed forces, General Electric is a major producer of aircraft and ordnance systems, jet engines, and other defence weapons. However, the job is far from being a "one-company" affair. Over 17,000 subcontractors and suppliers are contributing manpower and materials to G.E.'s defence production. This policy of spreading the defence effort is supported and encouraged by the military services. And, most important, many of those companies are classified as "small business."
I think that is an extremely important statement. This advertisement goes on to illustrate the benefits which accrue to the small town which has a subcontractor within its limits. The particular community which is pictured is a little place in Maine called Waterville. I would remind the minister that Maine is just across the border from the maritimes, and if subcontracts can be successfully let in Maine I think the same principle could be followed in this country. Subcontractors for small components for such things as aircraft engines, and an infinite number of items, could be set up in the maritimes.
This advertisement goes on to point out that General Electric jet subcontractors are numerous, and that 82 per cent of them are small businesses employing less than 500 people. That is an ideal state of affairs. If we could have our defence production coming from a large number of small factories in small areas, it would be about as safe as it would be possible to make it from aerial attack. It would serve as well as a great stimulant to the economy of many of the small communities across this country which, at the present time, are unable to absorb the natural increase in their population. Their young people are going off to Toronto, Montreal and a few other centres to work in the large war plants under unsatisfactory living conditions which largely stem from the building up of large unorganized cities, where great housing shortages exist today.

Mr. Chairman, I am not going to delay the house very long, but I have a few remarks I want to make on this general item of defence production. It is rather difficult to discuss the defence production estimates without getting into the field of national defence, because they are tied together very closely. The Department of National Defence is using the materials created or purchased by the defence production department. Nevertheless, the defence production department has a rather serious responsibility, not only to the defence effort but also to the economic future of Canada.
The minister has the power to create industry, regulate it and allocate it if the

circumstances warrant. In that connection what he creates and allocates now should be done with an eye to the future. I listened to the last speaker's plea for decentralization of industry, and it is not so far-fetched. While his suggestion that an atomic bomb might drop tonight on the minister's department and destroy the records is a bit far-fetched, nevertheless-

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: It would not be very serious if it did.

It would be a great loss to this country and, under present circumstances, perhaps to the world. When you look at world conditions today, the hon. member's plea in that regard was not far-fetched. A lot of people sit complacently and say, "Well, those things are happening in other parts of the world, but they cannot happen here." We are faced with an enemy that is moving on a global scale. If one looks at Korea and listens to the warnings we are getting that the armistice talks were only designed to allow the build-up of forces, then one realizes that things are not so good. Anything could happen. The top military brass who were a bit complacent, not in Canada but all over the world a few months ago, and who had high hopes of something developing from the peace talks that might prevent the return to what we have had for the last two years, do not seem to be as optimistic now. There are communist riots in Germany, while in the United States there are threats of strikes. It is all part of the same pattern.
I have discussed with the minister many times the necessity for dispersing our war industry across this country as much as possible. The extracts from the press read by the last speaker-we have all read them-are warnings that are being sounded by men who are very realistic. They have been warning the United States against too heavy a concentration of her war industries in any particular city. I think that is also true of Canada. It does not seem as if we are learning very much from the past, because we are continuing to centralize our industry in the two provinces of Ontario and Quebec. There is no need of going into all the facts and figures that we have gone into in the past. I think the present policy is extremely short-sighted, not only from the standpoint of the possibility of war; and the kind of war we are going to have in the future is something about which no one in this chamber has any illusions. It is not going to be a matter of front lines and of soldiers taking the brunt of the battle. It is going to be a strategic war to knock out your machine of production; and the civilian is really going to be in the front line. The more highly concentrated your industry and population are in one spot, the
Supply-Defence Production easier it is going to be to knock you out. There is no need of our putting our heads in the sand. As the world looks today, there is a possibility of that kind of thing developing. I do not think our enemies are backing up. I think they are moving on all fronts and are following a well-defined pattern. We should be preparing for that eventuality.
I can understand a country like the United States, which has perhaps reached her maximum in population, building around what she now has, such as around her power sites and so on. That development took place before the advent of the kind of world in which we are now living. But this country is young and it is growing. We have a large-scale immigration program.
