Unless we are destroyed by an eruption I think that program is going to continue to expand. This country is one of the last frontiers. It is the only place available to those from other countries whose whole machine of production has broken down and whose resources have run out. This is about the only part of the civilized world today to which those people can come to eke out an existence in a country that is highly civilized. We are going to attract a great many people in the next twenty years.
The minister is a good planner; he has proved that in the past. He is a good engineer, and engineers are practical people. I suggest to him that the allocation of defence industries should be done with an eye not only to keeping them widely dispersed in the event of war but also keeping in mind the future development of the country. I think it is a waste of money to build a large-scale war plant in Ontario or Quebec, under present circumstances; for in the event of there being no war or in the event of a war developing and terminating, there is waste of money in tearing it all down again. It is a simple matter today to reconvert a plant from war production to peacetime production. I think the minister should be looking at the other parts of the country where there is power or the possibility of obtaining power, with an eye to locating there plants that can be swung over in the future to care for the needs of the future.
I think in the last war we wasted a great deal of money by building plants in certain sections where they had to be torn down after the war. To go to an established industry and ask them to create an adjunct to that plant for war purposes, and to build it on land that is owned by that corporation, with a clause written into the agreement that in the event of that plant no longer being useful for that particular purpose it must be removed from that site and off that land

Supply-Defence Production if anyone else intends to use it, is a procedure that should not be adopted. That is something that happened in a great many cases, and millions and millions of dollars of our money went down the drain with respect to plants that could have been maintained even today. Many of the plants that we lost after the war were given away for 10 per cent of their total value; and five years later we find ourselves buying those plants back at 100 cents on the dollar, and at inflated prices. I cannot see anything that has happened since 1945 or 1948 to change that picture. I think the same thing is continuing today.
I know the minister and I have talked a good many times about this business of steel expansion in this country. I do not think his opinions differ greatly from my own on the question of expanding the steel industry. We are leaning too heavily on the arm of the United States. There is no reason in the world why we should not be expanding our own steel industry. It has been expanded some. I am thinking now in terms of basic steel. The minister in his statement this afternoon and yesterday indicated that if there is a strike in the United States all our planning is thrown completely out the window as a result of our inability to secure the necessary steel imports from the United States. We have iron ore in Labrador and coal in Nova Scotia; and it is good coal for metallurgical purposes. Most of the weapons that we are producing will not be used on this continent-at least that is my hope-but will be shipped out; we have all the ingredients for the making of raw steel at Sydney, at tidewater where it can be readily shipped at the closest point; and I hope if we are going to use these weapons, they will be used in that direction. Having regard to all these factors, I cannot understand why a greater expansion of steel in that area has not taken place.
Our leaning on the arm of the United States for our steel requirements is something I cannot understand. That country has a population of 150 million people. Its steel requirements are gigantic. There is no comparison at all between the amount of steel they have to use and what we have to use. We have 14 million people in this country, and have much greater resources for the production of raw steel. If the trend is to integrate the economy of this country with that of the United States, I cannot figure out why they or we want to drag the raw material all the way across the country in order to process it or fabricate it, when it could be done so easily down there at the


coast at much less cost, and be readily available to be shipped in the direction in which it is intended to be used.
As I say, I cannot understand that situation. I think that is something about which the Minister of Defence Production should have a showdown with the United States. We are today linked up in a common cause. Their interests are our interests in this industrial picture. We have to stand together or fall separately. There is no doubt about that. We on this North American continent are interdependent. I suggest that the minister should have a showdown with the United States on this matter of steel. Steel is basic to the whole economy of the country. It is a "must" in defence production. It is an actual need in our own internal economy. When steel production goes down or when there is a shortage or an interruption in the supply, everything in the country is affected, right down to your farm production.
If we are going to work this problem out together, I think we in this part of the North American continent are entitled to say that in that matter of basic steel the situation has been one of shortage from 1939 on. We have never had enough steel. Every time you raise the question of housing, vehicle production or defence production, you run into the question of the shortage of steel. I cannot understand why that situation should exist because we have on both coasts everything necessary to turn out steel in this country. Why we are not going ahead with that expansion I do not know. I know the minister has done his best to interest the steel companies of Canada. He has offered to put up a dollar for every dollar they expend in expansion. Some of them took up the offer to some extent; others did not touch it. This business of free enterprise being permitted to create that kind of chaos with regard to a basic material is something that should not happen under present circumstances. I understand the government's policy to be: as far as we are concerned we believe in free enterprise. That was the statement as I heard it. But the government is prepared to step in where free enterprise does not do the job. There is no hon. member in this house-I do not care where he sits-who can tell us that the basic steel industry have made the effort they should have to meet the requirements of this country since 1945. I will be charitable to them and write it down to those last seven years.
That is something in which you have to get production. You can talk about manpower. These are problems that are tricky. We talk about a lot of other things, but the matter of basic steel is the root of the whole

economy of this country. It is something that we should not fool with for a minute. If Dosco or Stelco or Algoma are not prepared to meet the requirements of this country in the matter of supplying basic steel, then the government should follow up the policy enunciated in this house and step in where they fail to meet our requirements, and that certainly has been true in basic steel.
The minister or others may say that I am arguing for my own end of the country. I am not doing that at all. I would be making the same argument if Ontario had what is required to turn out basic steel. I am not talking about the fabricating of it. A lot of it should be done there, particularly vehicles and munitions which are to be shipped out of this country to the NATO countries of Europe. To ship from that part of the country is the shortest haul, and a lot of it should be done there. I am thinking of this problem now in terms of being a Canadian. We are going to have to face this situation quicker than we expect or want to. We cannot make guns unless we have the steel. We can fool around with the problem of housing and with almost everything else, but not with the matter of supplying the NATO countries and our own country and helping out in other directions. It is not enough to say that we have a shortage of steel. Every effort should be made to meet that situation. I see it as a very serious problem at this time. I think it is one that requires consultation with the United States. If we cannot do it and do it quickly; if we cannot find the capital to do it, then our partner in this job of defence should help us, because the NATO countries are dependent on the North American continent for most of the munitions of war they will have to use in the event of trouble developing.
I would suggest that the minister's statements are merely statements of his inability to meet the steel requirements at this time.
I would like to see something better than that done. I believe it requires a conference of the United States and our own people. If the basic industries in this country are still not prepared to go ahead and meet our requirements, then the government should do it, and they should hang on to the plants when the war is over. Do not turn them over at 10 per cent of their value.
There are some questions I should like to ask on the steel end of the thing, but I am going to wait until we get to the proper item.
I thought I should say what I have at this time, because I think the hon. member for Queens, who just took his seat, knew what he was talking about. He is a man who went through the last war. He has a good war
Supply-Defence Production record. He is watching the thing, and all these matters are fresh in his mind. Much of what he said this afternoon should be hammered home in the minds of the general public. Things are not as good as we think they are. We are dealing with an enemy who is working all the time. He is moving on all fronts. He is using none of his own people at all; he is just slowly breaking down democracy and everything it stands for in every other country that he wants to soften up against the time when he puts over a right hook. We should get wise to it.
It is all right for the Minister of National Defence to rise and say, as I have heard him say several times, that our manpower commitments are met; we are doing all right; we are short a few in the air force. That is fine; we can raise all the men that are necessary and do everything else that is necessary, but if we have not the steel to make the munitions of war, we have nothing. Men in uniform are no good if they have nothing but their bare hands. We require the sinews of war, and; the sinews of war are steel over and above everything else.

The basic problem we are faced with is to produce the sinews of war with as little damage as possible to our economy. The problem is certainly not an easy one, and it is one that takes constant revision, constant planning and constant alteration of demands that have changed through circumstances which arise in this country.
I wish to speak on one or two matters which, since I come from one of the concentrated industrial areas of Canada, have been brought to my attention. The first one is this. There are a number of small businesses who write to me or complain to me because they have not the information which tells them how to go about submitting their productive capacity to the department. I know the machinery is all there, and whenever they write to me I can always put them in touch with the proper officer of the department; but I feel this is one thing the department might be doing as a start either through the manufacturers' association or the boards of trade or the chambers of commerce, so that every producer, no matter how small, would know how to go about getting in touch with the department and having what he can produce available at all times.
I feel that a survey of production, continuously revised, would be a useful thing to have; not only, of course, of big corporations whose productive ability is well known, but of the small two or three-man industries which can and frequently have produced very valuable material. I feel that one of the first things

Supply-Defence Production necessary is a production survey. I realize that the minister has been working on it; but judged by the complaints I get, it has not gone down to small industry the way it might have.
The second point I wish to mention is the allocation of metals under international agreements. We in this country have, through an international agreement, allocated our production chiefly of metals but also of many other scarce and wartime materials. There have been complaints by some industries that because our position as a manufacturing country is not fully understood by the United States a greater proportion of our metals has been allocated for international use than the economy should stand. Whether or not that criticism is just I am not in a position to say; but yesterday in New York a Canadian speaking on the same subject before the association of Canadian management stated that the Americans did not have a proper appreciation of the productive ability of this country. I mention this because people have complained to me about the extent of our commitments under this agreement. I realize that metals have to be shared; we have to share things with our partners. But I hope we will maintain enough for our own productivity.
The minister rightly stressed the desirability of avoiding controls. Nothing can destroy production more quickly, or with greater effect throw a monkey wrench into the war production of this country, than the reintroduction of a system of controls. Nothing could do so much damage, do it so quickly or decrease production to so great an extent. So I am glad to note that there is no thought of controls in the department at this time. There have been occasions, of course, where the allocation of scarce metals has been absolutely necessary, but I shall refer to that in a moment.
Recent developments at places like Kitim:, t have shown the great value of accelerated depreciation in these new developments. There are many developments the economic future of which may be questioned-and in this group I would not include Kitimat- where, if it were not for the accelerated depreciation feature, the erection and construction of new plants might not be commercially advisable.
The importance of letting business and industry work out their own production problems was also stressed, and is of paramount importance.
Then the flexibility of specifications is a matter that has been brought to my attention. Many industries have made reference to the rigidity of specifications for weapons and other materials for war purposes. No

one knows better than I how important is the over-all efficiency in the production of a weapon when men's lives depend upon it. As an example of the rigidity of specifications I would refer to a six weeks' delay in a program for the production of radar sets because the name plate did not meet the specifications of one of the services. I feel that is carrying rigidity of specifications altogether too far.
In his speech the minister made reference to the interchangeability of specifications. I would hope that this would also include the interchange of information connected with atomic weapons. It is most important that this be done, because the fact that we work in one compartment while the United States works in another in this extremely important field is not to the advantage of either country. I would hope therefore that the interchange of information at all levels on atomic projects has been arranged.
I come now to the question of standardization of weapons. While I realize that this is not the minister's responsibility, nevertheless the problem is one in which he is vitally concerned. I mention one instance of this, namely the production of the -50 calibre Browning machine gun. As many hon. members can testify from personal experience, if this weapon is not obsolete then certainly it is now becoming so. The Royal Air Force, and later the Royal Canadian Air Force, held the belief that the 20 millimetre cannon was a far -ore effective weapon. Because of our agreement with the United States we have now standardized on the -50 calibre machine gun. While the factory in which it is being produced is most efficient, and while the production of the weapons will no doubt be carried out in excellent fashion, nevertheless the whole question as to whether in this day it is a desirable weapon, with aircraft travelling at greatly accelerated speeds and having much greater hitting power than at the time of the last war, is one with which the House of Commons should concern itself.
Not only are production and the cost of production matters of interest to the taxpayers but-and this is more important-we must always keep in mind that men's lives depend upon the effectiveness of the weapons we produce. As I said earlier, I realize that the choice of the weapon rests with the Department of National Defence, and that the Minister of Defence Production produces only that which he is asked to produce. But I would hope that before the close of this debate there might be some further discussion on this matter.

Then turning to the production of steel; while we hope next year to have production to a point a third greater than the production of 1950, nevertheless the production of basic steel has not kept pace with our economic growth in other lines. Despite the fact that the Steel Company of Canada, Algoma Steel, and Dosco have added blast furnaces and increased basic steel production in their plants, the production of basic steel has not kept pace with our economic growth.
I believe the producers of the rarer but extremely important metals, such as nickel, tungsten and cobalt, all of which are in extremely short supply, and which are essential war materials, are doing everything possible to make the supply adequate for our needs. There is, however, one point I would place before the minister, and that is with reference to scrap iron and scrap steel. There is an enormous amount of scrap metal available, but apparently so far an all-out drive is not being made to see that this scrap metal is made available for our basic steel mills. Scrap metal is what the steel makers call the mine above the ground I feel that the people of Canada are not aware of the importance of the scrap iron that might be available, and that a greater effort should be made to collect this and channel it to the steel mills.
The minister rightly suggested that next to the production of aircraft our electronics production constitutes a major effort. I have had the opportunity of seeing what strides we are making in this connection. This is highly skilled work, and 1 believe the percentage of professional engineers on any assembly line turning out electronic products would probably be higher than in connection with any other work being done in Canada. Unfortunately engineers are not available in as great numbers as they should be. With our modern aircraft having its weapons almost completely fired by electronic means and in many cases the projectiles being guided by electronic means, this side of our defence effort should be pushed to its utmost limit. Canadians seem to have a particular skill for electronics work. For some reason or another Canadian workers, Canadian engineers and Canadian designers seem to have a penchant for electronics and the design and operation of instruments using this principle. I am glad to see that next to aircraft it is considered as our second line of production, and I hope everything possible will be done to increase it still further. I would hope to see us producing in Canada such weapons as the new ground-to-aircraft guided projectile which has met with such tremendous success in the United States. In my opinion we are not using 55704-174J

speechtext:
Before you ask the house to approve this motion for second reading, may I point out that there is a total of sixty of these bills with respect to which the motion for second reading is being moved at this time. So far as these sixty bills are concerned, the printed evidence has been distributed. I have not had time to read the evidence in all sixty but I have looked over the evidence in a number of them, and I find that it conforms to the type of evidence that usually comes before us in connection with these measures. There is a monotonous degree of similarity about them. In case after case we have the story of detectives being called in to get the evidence. In fact in a good many of the applications that we have before us tonight there is one particular pair of detectives who get the evidence time and time again. Indeed, the evidence they get is so much alike one wonders how they keep it straight in their own minds.
I have expressed the opinion before in a number of ways that I do not feel this is the way to be handling these or any other divorce bills. I regret very much that parliament has not yet agreed to my proposal to transfer

them to the exchequer court, or has not found some other way to deal with them. As long as this practice is followed by parliament-and by the will of parliament, which I think is wrong-we have no alternative but to grant the divorces where the required evidence is forthcoming. I still feel it is the wrong way to deal with these cases. That is not to reflect on the hon. gentlemen of the other place who do the job. I point out, however, that we do not do a job on these bills. This House of Commons just passes them en masse as we are doing at this time. I hope that even yet parliament will come to the point where we will find some other way to deal with divorce cases. I ask hon. members to give more thought to this matter. I ask them to consider the opinions that are being expressed in newspapers and magazines throughout the country, and I hope the day is not far distant when we will make up our minds that parliament is not the place to adjudicate on individual divorce cases.
Motion agreed to and bills read the second time.

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Tuesday, May 27, consideration in committee of Bill No. 62, to incorporate Boundary Pipeline Corporation- Mr. Larson-Mr. Beaudoin in the chair.
On section 1-Incorporation.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to make some remarks on this bill. It seems to me that we face a rather strange situation. Since the bill was introduced there have been speeches made against it which to me seemed to have points of substance and arguments which were worth meeting. But I understand practically no answer of any kind has been made since the bill was introduced. I wish to deal with it mainly from the point of view of what I understand to be the interests and wishes of the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, to which this incorporation would seem to go counter. I repeat that it seems strange to me that we should be debating this measure twice a week, and that it is left almost entirely to those who are opposed to it to speak. I do not know whether the measure is considered by those who support it to be of such outstanding excellence that it needs no support at all, but certainly it does not seem to me to be in that category.
The point, of course, is a very simple one. This Boundary pipe line is proposing to bring natural gas to Winnipeg, and then take it south. The sponsors, I understand, are Regina men; and the argument, which I shall endeavour to develop at some length later, is that their proposal is unsound because it
Boundary Pipeline Corporation is admitted that within the foreseeable future there is not going to be more than one pipe line. If, in fact, gas is taken to Manitoba and then taken south, this part of Canada will be left to what can be obtained from the United States, and at the present time that would be largely from Texas.
As I said a moment ago, there are two possible routes for this Alberta gas to take. One is to go to Winnipeg, then south to Minnesota; the other is to go to Winnipeg, then on to Ontario and Quebec. It seems to me that quite apart from the advantage of having this gas go to the central provinces, the latter route has this additional advantage, in that it does something to lessen that feeling of separateness which we had in Canada for so long. It lessens that area in the middle which, for a long time made the country seem like a pair of spectacles. Every enterprise that lessens that separateness of the two parts of Canada seems to me worth while in itself, and this would be an additional enterprise to the railways, woods operations and mineral operations which are filling up that interval and making that gap less obvious than it used to be.
As I say, if Boundary Pipeline gets incorporation, and if the province of Alberta allows the gas to be exported, and if the gas is taken to Manitoba and then south, central Canada will be left to the tender mercies of the United States, particularly of Texas. I believe it is relevant, not only relevant but important, for us to try to assess the likelihood of our getting gas on any basis which we could regard as sure from the United States. Happily, we do not have to guess what the attitude of the United States is, because there is considerable evidence. I wish to stress this evidence. I believe it has been given to the committee before, but the very fact that we are meeting here again tonight to debate this measure shows that it needs to be stressed again. I propose to stress it again, and 1 propose to read from a judgment of the federal power commission in an application of the Panhandle Eastern Pipeline Company for permission to export gas to Canada for the Union Gas Company of Ontario. The judgment is dated August 31, 1951 and I shall read from it.
Before I do so, I should like to stress this point which we should not fail to bear in mind. We live in the greatest amity with our friends to the south of the line. We are extremely like them in many ways, and it is perhaps the happiest circumstance of our life that our relations with them are as they are. But we should not blind ourselves to the fact that they are hard-headed business

Boundary Pipeline Corporation people. We can see evidence today, in connection with tariff matters, that they are beginning to revert to some of the exclusionist policies from which we suffered so much years ago. This judgment I am going to read- nobody can complain about it-shows that they are going to think about themselves. In thinking about themselves, they may not be able to think about us as much as we would like.
I now read from this judgment of August 31, 1951:
It is obvious from the foregoing that, in view of the demonstrated requirements of customers within the United States and the present designed capacity of the Panhandle system, no natural gas is available for exportation on a firm basis at this time.
I repeat those words "on a firm basis at this time", because anything less than a firm basis is really of no value. I shall have occasion later on to refer to what was said by Mr. Gemmell, minister of mines of Ontario. One of the points he stressed was that there was no use getting gas unless they got a guarantee of its continuance. It is better not to get it at all, because if a business community is built up on the basis of receiving a supply which is suddenly cut off one could imagine not only the economic confusion which would arise but the great bitterness and strife which would be in the greatest degree undesirable. I believe we have faced the fact that for us to export to the United States and then suddenly cut it off-when the shoe is on the other foot-is something that could hardly be contemplated. The United States, with its mudh greater strength, will certainly take that view.
I continue to read from the judgment:
The record, therefore, shows that the proposed exportation will not be consistent with the public interest. The application in this docket will, therefore, be dismissed without prejudice.
That seems to go a very long way to show that Ontario and Quebec would be in a most uncomfortable position if they were relying on the export of gas from the United States.
There have been other rulings to that effect, and I shall quote from another. I have a ruling on another application by Panhandle in 1946 for the right to export gas from the United States to Canada near the city of River Rouge, Michigan, to be delivered to the Union Gas Company of Canada. Here is an extract from the judgment:
No deliveries of natural gas shall be made to Union during the months of January, February, March, November and December in any year during the term of this authorization.
That is a comforting thought, that the months you could not get gas would be the very ones for which you needed it most. The


reason is obvious, because those are the months the United States needs it most. The judgment goes on:
Delivery of natural gas to Union shall be curtailed or interrupted whenever, and to the extent, required for the protection of deliveries of natural gas, either for immediate consumption or for storage, to any and all of the applicant's customers in the United States.
That is very clear. I continue to read:
The authorization hereby granted shall not constitute ground or justification for any refusal by applicant to transport or sell natural gas to any person or municipality at any time during the term hereof, either for consumption in the United States by such person or municipality or for storage, or for resale for ultimate public consumption in the United States for domestic, commercial, industrial, or any other use, it being the intent of this authorization that at all times, persons and municipalities in the United States are to receive preferential service over that to Union;
That is the Union Gas Company of Ontario, the Canadian company. I do not see how we can complain about it, but we certainly would be extremely foolish if we did not take the warning that is there contained and govern ourselves accordingly. In this connection it is interesting to note that apparently there are some large cities in the United States which are not yet fully served. Philadelphia is mentioned as one of them. As I say, without labouring the point, I think the committee will agree that we are on notice that even if we can get gas from the United States, it will be on the strictly limited condition which I have just read.
In the light of this situation I would have thought that the committee which was appointed to consider this matter-that is to say, the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines-would have wanted to try to get to the bottom of this thing and would have shown the patience and consideration which most committees show and which are the very genius of our whole system and of this House of Commons. Hon. members opposite often have to listen to speeches from us on this side of the house which they find exceedingly tiresome, and we have to do the same with regard to them; but it is understood that that is part of our system. Yet in this committee it seems to me the closure was used. Although the government has the right to use closure, it has certainly not been applied during my few years of experience in this house, and I understand that it has been applied but few times since it was first introduced forty years ago. But what I call closure-and I think it can be fairly described as closure-was used in this committee.
I should like to read briefly from the minutes of proceedings of the committee, just

to indicate what I mean. I am reading from page 73 of the minutes of proceedings of Thursday, April 24, 1952:

that sufficient evidence has been obtained for the committee to decide as to the economic practicability of the pipe line under consideration; and that the question be put on the preamble without further examination of the witness. After discussion and the question having been put on the said motion, it was agreed to on the following division.
I think that was a pity, because it seems to me that the genius of this whole system of ours is that there is a certain amount of forbearance shown by members with each other. I am on the defence expenditures committee, and a good many things have happened with which I have not agreed; and I think I have said a good many things with which the chairman did not agree and with which other members of the committee did not agree. But the chairman has been patient. We have sometimes been voted down. That cannot be helped. But we have been allowed to have our day in court and to say what we wanted to say.
Last Tuesday when this bill was before the committee for consideration the matter came into prominence because the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine raised it on a kind of long distance question of privilege which he reached 'with difficulty. I would imagine that he may have made parliamentary history. I greatly doubt if there have been many questions of privilege which lasted so long. At any rate it was interesting while it lasted. What struck me was that he moved this resolution, as I understood it, because he felt that the hon. member for Calgary West was not cross-examining the witness. I had probably better read his exact words. As reported at page 2631 of Hansard of May 27, he said:
The point is that the hon. member for Calgary West at that time was not in fact cross-examining at all. He was simply trying to get on the record, through the medium of that witness, figures that had been prepared by others.
My -comment on that is this. The comment was made in this house the other evening that actually the hon. member for Calgary West was acting as a witness. The hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine complained that the hon. member for Calgary West was acting as if he was a witness. In that connection the hon. member for Victoria (Ont.) who was also a member of the committee said:
He was as much a witness as Herring was.
Mr. Herring was the witness who was being examined. Without going into the niceties of the matter, and without going into the question as to whether the hon. member for Calgary West was in fact cross-examining
Boundary Pipeline Corporation the witness or whether he was in fact giving some evidence himself, may I say that, as we all know, he is a man with considerable knowledge of these things. Whether he was in fact observing the niceties of crossexamination or was introducing some information himself, I would have thought the committee would have been glad indeed to be informed and that the objection which apparently was felt so strongly by some members of the committee would not have constituted a serious objection at all.
I should like to read a little bit more from what took place in the committee because I think it is of some importance. I think there is one inescapable difficulty with all committees. We all know that they have to be chosen on a proportionate basis. We all know that they have a government majority. That fact cannot be escaped. We all know that, by and large, the government majority is going to vote as is desired. I am not criticizing that practice. All I am saying is that the whole genius of our system is that the rights of the minority are protected by their having their day in court, in other words by their being able to express their views.
I am just coming along now to the point at which closure was applied in the committee, and I think that is a matter of great importance. We arrived at the point where there was some question as to whether the hon. member for Calgary West was in fact cross-examining the witness or whether he was giving evidence. I read from the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, commencing at the bottom of page 76:

Mr. Chairman, if I may be permitted a word; I do not think anyone wants to cut out discussion here.
I think that remark was in answer to the suggestion by the hon. member for Calgary West that perhaps the committee was not as ready to listen as they might have been. To continue:

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I do not think anyone wants to cut out discussion here and I think the hon. member will himself agree that at the last session of the committee that probably a wider latitude was given than is usual in matters of this kind. After our previous meeting it was ruled that Mr. Herring should have an opportunity of bringing in a certain statement, a report which he was to table. He was to produce that statement; I think it was Mr. Nickle who at that time said he would like to know whether Mr. Herring could give evidence as to whether it was economically feasible to run a pipe line from Winnipeg eastward to the province of Ontario, or what his views were. If that evidence can be given today, and if a cross-examination can then be confined to that statement, to the statement which is to be put in by Mr. Herring, I think we might very well get along in that manner without anyone being prejudiced.

Boundary Pipeline Corporation

It is the right in any committee, anywhere, for any member to express his opinion, quite apart from his right to cross-examine witnesses: so I suggest that we get on with the business and if the matter comes up later on we can deal with it.
Notwithstanding that, however, there apparently was a certain amount of uneasiness. Then we come to page 86 where the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine is reported as follows:

Mr. Chairman, we have on the one hand the evidence that was given by Mr. Herring at the request of the committee, supported by telegrams, and we have the evidence on Mr. Herring's statement that the information in the telegrams was obtained from responsible persons; on the other hand, we have no evidence except the statement of a member of the committee here-he is certainly entitled to express views, or to express his opinion as a member of the committee-the only evidence we have is the evidence submitted by Mr. Herring.
Then the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine makes this motion:
I move at this stage that the committee has obtained sufficient evidence to decide on the economic practicability of the pipeline under consideration and that the question be now put on the preamble without further examination of witnesses.
Then the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra said this:

-I am somewhat at a loss to understand why Mr. Cannon should make a motion of that type which in effect stops any further crossexamination.
In other words, Mr. Chairman, as you see closure was applied. The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra continued:
Surely, we are here as reasonable men trying to get this story before the committee. It may be that it is taking longer than some of the members think it should but we will have another hour of sitting this morning. It is most unusual in my experience for a member on a particular bill to get up and move that the discussion be shut off. Now, this is not a party matter. It does not involve any question of policy. Surely, the committee.members are in favour of getting full information. It seems very strange that we should have someone rushing in to protect that particular charter.
I am not protecting it.

In effect that is what it is, by preventing any further cross-examination.
I will not pursue this any further, Mr. Chairman, but I will come back to point out what I said at the outset, that I cannot understand, first of all, why nobody, or practically nobody ever stands up to support this measure in the house. Second, I cannot understand why it would not have been agreeable to all concerned to let the examination go on. Surely we were seeking for truth in the matter. I do suggest that the proceedings of the committee were, to put it mildly, most unfortunate and most regrettable. I should like to say that my experience in other committees is that every effort is made by the chairman not to arbitrarily cut off anyone who has a view to express on the matter before the committee. That


is not to say the chairmen always allow you to discuss everything you think you should be allowed to discuss. I am not saying that, but I do say in general the chairmen are considerate, and I do not know of any case in which this has been done. If other people do know it might be interesting to taring it up, because I think to have virtually what can be described only as closure used in committee is a very unfortunate matter.
I said at the outset that the reason I was taking part in this debate and trying to sustain an argument against the measure was that the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, through their government representatives, have expressed themselves in such clear fashion. That being so, it seems to me there is the strongest onus on us, at any rate, to stop, look and listen before we go ahead with something which, so far as I can see from the record, is entirely inimical to their interest. I hold in my hand two statements by Mr. Gemmell, the minister of mines in the province of Ontario. I also have a statement by the premier of Quebec. I want to put these on the record. They are very clearly expressed. There is no doubt in their minds as to what the interests of their provinces demand. Incidentally, Mr. Chairman, we will find, particularly in the case of the statement by the premier of Quebec, a strong feeling that this is not merely a matter which is in the interests of Ontario and Quebec, but it is a kind of national matter which is in the interests of Canada regarded as a whole.
Here is what Mr. Gemmell said on January 26 last, as reported in the Globe and Mail:
Ottawa, Jan. 21.-Even if it has to be subsidized a pipeline should be built to bring Alberta natural gas to Ontario and Quebec, provincial mines minister Gemmell said here today.
In Ottawa to attend the annual meeting of the Canadian institute of mining and metallurgy, Mr. Gemmell declared that a west-to-east natural gas pipeline was as important to national prosperity today as the C.P.R. was when it was started in the 1870's.
That I find interesting, and I anticipate what he says in a later statement that I am going to read, because he speaks again of the foresight of those who built the Canadian Pacific Railway through Canada even though it would have been shorter, and I suppose cheaper, to build it through the United States.
I continue reading from Mr. Gemmell:
He envisaged the gas heating of homes, factories and office buildings throughout Ontario as well as the use of gas to generate the motive power of thousands of industries. He believed, he said, that there would be an initial market in eastern Canada for 300 million cubic feet of gas per day, rising to 500 million cubic feet in five years and one billion cubic feet per day in ten years.

At present an Alberta government board is entertaining a proposal by the Canadian Delhi Petroleum Company whereby the firm's subsidiary, Trans-Canada Pipe Lines, would build a pipeline to follow the C.P.R. main line from the Alberta oil and gas fields to Toronto and Montreal. The line would cost $250 million, take three years to build and would require 750,000 tons of steel. Such a tonnage of such a scarce commodity could only be obtained on general agreement that construction of the pipeline was vital to national defence. Mr. Gemmell says it is.
Natural gas is much cheaper than the manufactured gas such as is retailed in Toronto by the Consumers Gas Company. Manufactured gas costs roughly $2 per 1,000 cubic feet whereas natural gas would cost in Toronto $1.10 to $1.15 per 1,000 cubic feet. What is more, its heat is such as to bring a kettle to the boil twice as quickly as manufactured gas would.
I have to take his word for that; I do not understand gas well enough to express an opinion myself. The article continues:
It is believed that if Alberta gas were piped east, the Consumers' Gas Company would distribute it in the Toronto area.
If Alberta gas is so much cheaper and could be delivered to Ontario so readily, what is holding it up, anyone might ask. Mr. Gemmell gave the answer. The Alberta government will not let gas out of Alberta until it is satisfied that enough would be left to supply Alberta's present and potential needs. Naturally, Alberta wants the gas to build up industries of its own as well as to heat the homes of its own citizens. Thus, export to other provinces is a secondary consideration.
For these reasons, the Alberta petroleum resources board is giving long consideration to the Delhi application for permission to pipe gas to Ontario and Quebec. Some experts say Alberta has plenty of gas and to spare but the board is investigating. And when and if the Alberta board gives the pipeline the nod, its promoters must next get permission from the board of transport commissioners here to build the line. It is thought, however, that if the Alberta board agrees, the transport commissioners will not make any difficulties.
An alternative suggestion, Mr. Gemmell said, is that if Alberta would allow gas to be piped into the western United States, Ontario might draw an equal volume from the Texas wells. Gas is now being piped north from Texas to Detroit and thence into Windsor and western Ontario.
Mr. Gemmell declared the provincial government was wholly opposed to any deal of this kind. In the first place, he said, it was very doubtful that the United States authorities would agree to supply Ontario with a firm uninterrupted volume of gas, day in and day out, year by year.
"Secondly," he said, "there is the question of the national interest. Sir John A. Macdonald could have built the C.P.R. through the United States. It would have been a shorter route. But he had it built through Canada and subsidized the C.P.R. to build it that way and I think most Canadians will agree that he was right. We in Ontario are sticking to the view that a strictly national use of our national resources is the best thing for Canada in the long run."
Mr. Gemmell suggested that the pipeline company might need a capital subsidy to build its line, although when the company sought a parliamentary charter a few years ago it made no mention of a subsidy. He believed that in the national interest and particularly in respect of defence, the federal government would be justified in applying public funds to such a purpose. He made it clear,
Boundary Pipeline Corporation with a laugh, that he was talking about a federal subsidy, not a subsidy from the Ontario government, of which he is a member.
The proposed Trans-Canada pipeline would be of 30 inches diameter from the Alberta fields to Winnipeg and 24 inches thence to Toronto and Montreal. It would bring the gas to western Ontario where the old gas wells in Dawn township, between Sarnia and Chatham, present a ready made storage basin. These wells were pumped out years ago and are now used by the Union Gas Company of Chatham to store the gas it buys from Texas.
Mr. Gemmell said these old wells were one of the best gas storage basins in the world. They are needed because gas, like electricity, is used more in the winter than in summer.
I have another statement from Mr. Gemmell that I should like to read if I have time, but first of all I should like to read a statement by the premier of Quebec dated March 28:
Premier Duplessis said today a Texas firm and an Alberta firm want to export natural gas to this province, but Quebec has decided that if any is to be imported, it will come from Alberta.
The premier told his weekly press conference that representatives of the U.S. and Canadian pipeline construction firms had been in touch with him.
He said nothing had been decided yet on whether pipelines will be built into Quebec.
But he said Quebec preferred to import gas from Alberta because it would support a Canadian industry . . .
He said representatives of United States and Canadian pipeline construction firms had been in touch with him about the possibilities of exporting natural gas.
The premier said nothing had yet been decided as to whether pipelines would be built or not into Quebec province. But he said, if natural gas is to be imported it will not be U.S. gas.
The premier said Quebec preferred to import the gas from Alberta because it was preferable to support a Canadian industry, not subject "to a foreign authority."
Well, you will agree that this statement I have read bears out what I said at the outset, that responsible authorities in Ontario and Quebec believe that it will be most precarious and unwise to rely upon sources south of the international boundary line, and that the proper course, as soon as the province of Alberta makes up its mind that sufficient gas can be spared, is that that gas should be brought to eastern Canada.
So I wish just to review briefly the arguments I have made to date. It is agreed that there is to be only one line at the present time. It is agreed-indeed, it is not only agreed; it is in the record-that the present applicant is proposing to bring gas to Winnipeg, and then take it south. That would mean the central provinces would have to negotiate with Texas.
I have read the judgments of the United States authorities which say that gas can only be exported subject to American requirements. I have pointed out that there are United States cities, notably the city of

Boundary Pipeline Corporation Philadelphia, which are short of gas at the present time. Therefore it seems to me selfevident that the position of the provinces of Ontario and Quebec is such that it is an imperative need for them that, as soon as gas is available from Alberta, it should be brought, not to Winnipeg, and then turned south at the border but that it should be brought straight east.
Mr. Gemmell had some other things to say on this matter which are worth reading, because they underline what I have already placed on the record; and these statements were made two months later, when he was two months wiser and had a certain amount of additional information. This is his statement on March 6, 1952:
Despite the bright future for natural gas in eastern Canada, not one Canadian-owned firm has shown interest in piping it from Alberta, mines minister Gemmell said yesterday.
"Shall we always have to depend on our neighbour's eagerness to capitalize on our lack of imagination and daring to develop our country's resources?" he inquired of a Kiwanis club luncheon at the Royal York.
"Or shall we, as Canadians, decide once and for all that we could do this job all by ourselves and reap a greater share of the benefits to be derived from the exploitation of this, the most promising country on earth?"
That, by the way, leads me to point out that I understand that although this application is made by a group of Regina men, actually behind them is a United States pipeline engineering firm known as Fish Engineering Corporation of Houston, Texas. I am the last one in the world to object to United States capital coming in here. But I am referring to this view expressed by the minister of mines of the province of Ontario, which has some bearing on this present application. The article continues:
Noting that a decision on five applications to pipe natural gas out of Alberta is expected late this month or early in April, Mr. Gemmell expressed the fear that it might all go first to the U.S. and that the one company proposing an allCanadian pipeline-the U.S.-controlled Trans-Canada Pipe Lines-might be turned down.
While there was something to be said for the view that it was better to pipe Alberta gas first to the U.S. and then into eastern Canada, the mines minister suggested that, in the long run, an all-Canadian project would be better. "No matter how you look at it," he declared, "the future of Canada, and certainly the future of eastern Canada depends to a large extent on the decisions to be made by the Alberta conservation board, the Alberta government and the board of transport commissioners at Ottawa. I, for one, am inclined to believe that the interests of the majority of Canadians will not be forgotten at the time of decision.
"We need natural gas in eastern Canada . . . Natural gas will replace hydro as our source of power in the years to come ... We need a guaranteed supply of natural gas in northern and eastern Canada. I should like to underline that word guaranteed."

The view that gas could be brought more easily from Texas, Mr. Gemmell suggested, snagged on the word guaranteed. Already one application by an American firm had been turned down by the U.S. government, and another withdrawn because rejection had been indicated.
"In view of the Washington attitude toward Canada's reciprocal agreement relative to the St. Lawrence seaway, the question is raised as to the dispatch with which the U.S. would consummate the proposed natural gas deal," he said. "Further, no necessity exists whatever on Canada's part for a natural gas reciprocal agreement. An all-Canadian pipeline to serve Canadians awaits only government approval.
"Proponents of the reciprocal agreement theory suggest there would be no difficulty encountered in having the U.S. Natural Gas Act amended . . . They say, in effect, that U.S. citizens have a warm spot in their hearts for Canadians and would not raise a finger to stop natural gas from running past their non-supplied homes as long as we, in Canada, put it to good use. Well, that's a little hard to believe."
The all-Canadian line, Mr. Gemmell said, would serve over 5 million people, many more than any of the other projects being considered by the Alberta board.
An initial market of 200 million cubic feet a day is anticipated, rising in three years to 365 million and in 10 to a billion.
Cost for the heating of homes in Toronto by natural gas would be only about half that of manufactured gas, and its availability would be a "tremendous" stimulant for new industry in Ontario and Quebec.
I shall not repeat the arguments I have made; but I will say it seems to me that those who are supporting this bill are under a strong onus to stand up and answer these arguments being made by responsible public men in the governments of Ontario and Quebec. These men have studied the matter; it is vital to them. They have expressed their views definitely; and I think it is an undignified spectacle for this House of Commons to go on with this one-sided debate -if we could call it a debate, at all-this onesided monologue, when arguments, serious arguments by serious people, have been put forward which, so far as I am aware, no one has attempted to answer. However modest we may be, however unworthy we may feel ourselves to be, we are not quite at the point where there is no need at all to answer arguments made. And even if hon. members do not think it is worth, their while to answer us, they might think it is worth while to answer the governments of Ontario and Quebec, whose views I have tried to express.
Therefore I say that in the light of the evidence before this House of Commons, no one in the house has any right whatever to vote for this measure.
(Translation):

Mr. Speaker, like my neighbour, the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) and my good friends of the Social Credit, I am glad that the Creator has put gas deposits in the area making up Alberta

today and that following the discovery of such deposits clever and courageous people have undertaken to develop them.
There lies in western Canada . . .
So states Mr. Gerard Gardner in his book "A study of the Economic Value of the Canadian Far North"-Mr. Gardner is a Ph.D. of the Universite de Paris and a professor at the School of Higher Commercial Studies, in Montreal.
-a vast strip of land capable of yielding oil and gas. This strip extends from the American border, which it crosses, up to to Arctic ocean, to the north; from the Canadian shield, in the east, to the Rocky mountains, in the west. This vast region covers 891,000 square miles of sedimentary ground. This strip is so vast that Texas, California, Oklahoma, Kansas and Louisiana laid upon it would not cover it completely. These five states are indeed the biggest producers of gas and oil in the United States and their present reserves and their production to date amount to an approximate 50 billion barrels. This does not necessarily mean that the Canadian area contains riches comparable to the resources of those five American states, but serious and justified hopes may be entertained with regard to future developments. We might say that deposits already discovered in that strip of land in Canada have reserves of over a billion barrels.
The whole Canadian people are bound to benefit from this providential windfall which at the present time gladdens the hearts of the people and the government of Alberta. But, in order to benefit fully from this new wealth, it is important to have it distributed in a judicious and adequate manner, so as to serve Canada first.
We must not consider only the present, but also the future of this country, which may be foreseen as a brilliant one.
In my opinion, the Alberta government has shown wisdom and foresight by establishing, in 1938, the conservation board, in order, among other things, to regulate production and to protect the oil fields against the disastrous fires that were then occurring in the Turner valley.
I hope it will continue in that direction and will ensure that the resources of the province will be developed to the benefit of all Canadians.
On the other hand, we should investigate carefully the petitions for charters submitted for our consideration by companies anxious to organize the transportation of natural gas. During the past few years we have been called upon to examine several bills like the one we are discussing tonight.
In October, 1949, we dealt with bills relating to the Alberta Natural Gas Company and to the Prairie Transmission Lines Limited.
Those bills were not passed and had to be submitted again at the following session.
Boundary Pipeline Corporation
The main point of division among members at that time was the matter of deciding whether we should compel those companies to build their pipe lines entirely on Canadian soil, so as to serve our cities and rural areas before those of the United States.
These private bills won the support of leading government spokesmen and of some cabinet members who recommended their speedy approval, though they were vigorously opposed by Progressive Conservative and socialist members.
The hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Murphy) pointed out last Friday that the Liberal party is in favour of the exportation of Alberta gas to the United States, but the provincial Liberal party in Alberta vigorously opposes the idea.
There lies an amazing contradiction which prompts us to ask ourselves whether the higher interests of the nation are adequately protected by the party now in power. It has been said in this house that the sponsors of the Boundary Pipeline Corporation, though residents of Regina, are in fact nothing else but dummies, used as a screen by the Fish Engineering Corporation of Houston, Texas.
I would like to know what are the purposes of this company in thus hiding behind these men. What booty are they looking for and who will be their victim? We must proceed with great care.
This very company is also closely connected with the Prairie Transmission Lines Limited.
I do not think that it would be wise to grant this charter.
The Interprovincial Company whose pipe line goes from Alberta to Superior, Wisconsin, is at the present time carrying adequate quantities of natural gas. However these supplies, because of the growing industrial importance of Ontario and Quebec, will not be sufficient to provide the whole of these two provinces' needs should this company be incorporated, and should it receive the right of installing a pipe line of only 16 inches in diameter. In this way we shall lose a further opportunity of obtaining the gas we need. It is only natural that our first concern should be for our country and that we should work towards its advancement.
In the article I was quoting from a while ago, Mr. Gardner writes further:
To find gas and oil and take it from the earth is not enough. The great problem, which is the same all over the north, is to transport this gas or oil by pipeline to the south since there is no possibility of consuming it on the spot. The most readily reached markets are those of the American middle-west and central states. I am not concerned with

Supply-Defence Production the question of transporting gas or oil towards American or Canadian markets, but we have here facts which are of paramount importance in our economy. Business men should follow most closely everything that is done in this connection. The construction of pipelines would bring great changes to the economics of gas and oil.
It is interesting to note that:
Oil production in northern Alberta, in 1950, reached 28,200 barrels for the Normandville field (one well), 6,206 barrels for the Whitelaw field (one well), while the Bolloque lake field yielded only 753 barrels, this well having been abandoned later on.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hour for private and public bills having expired, the house will resume consideration of the business under discussion at six o'clock.

The house in committee of supply, Mr. Beaudoin in the chair.
DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION A-Department-
79. Departmental administration and payments to Canadian Commercial Corporation and other corporate agencies for services provided in connection with defence purchasing and production, $7,332,492.

Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose at six o'clock I was about to discuss some of the problems of aircraft production. I think the one thing the country is interested in is when we can expect delivery of the weapons of defence in substantial numbers. We have really just arrived today at the end of our tooling-up program. We are about to produce. Nothing is worth anything until production gets going and the weapons of defence are delivered in numbers to the fighting services who may use them. I realize this is difficult. I realize that a great number of things we have had to produce have been new and have not been produced before. Apparently in all democracies there is a chronic shortage of machine tools. Engineers tell me that their idea of heaven is a place where there are enough machine tools for everybody to have one with which to work, but apparently the shortage of machine tools in Canada today is still chronic.
We are a long way from heaven.

Apparently so. It may or may not be fortunate that we are a long way from heaven, but we still have a shortage of machine tools. Coming to defence production, and with particular reference to the A. V. Roe Company, may I say as a member in opposition to the government that I think

this company has been subjected to a great deal of unwarranted criticism. The A. V. Roe Company started virtually from scratch. First of all they endeavoured to design and then produce three things, the Orenda engine, the CF-100 and the jet liner. For a well established aircraft company to have tackled these three projects at the same time would have been a major operation; but for a company which was in its formative stage to attempt these three things was almost a heroic venture.
Hon. members may think that the design and the production of a prototype of an aircraft or a new jet engine is a difficult thing, but compared with making that prototype an. item on a production line I feel that the design and development of the prototype is comparatively simple. It was in the hiatus period between the testing of the prototype and putting the engine or aircraft on a production basis that the trouble took place. In part I blame the government for the reason that they did not fully appreciate the difficulties. The Minister of Defence Production probably did, but the Minister of National Defence certainly did not, and the Canadian people have become rather disenchanted with this establishment because of the glowing statements which were made when the prototypes of the Orenda engine, the CF-100 and the jet liner were first tested.
When the first CF-100 was test flown two years ago, I believe, there was an unfortunate incident. It was unfortunate in this way, that when a new aircraft is being tested and test flown for the first time it is generally the most-I will not say "secret"-nerve-wracking performance. When the aircraft is not only a new aircraft being test flown for the first time but has new engines in it, then it becomes a doubly nerve-wracking procedure. Not only are millions of dollars of effort riding on the aircraft but the very lives of the flight crew and test pilot are involved. As somebody has explained to me, test flying a new aircraft with new engines is like a woman having her first child. She does not want an audience. When this new aircraft was being flown for the first time the Minister of National Defence and a large contingent of top brass appeared at Malton for the accouchement, and the flight crew were so annoyed at what had happened that they very nearly refused to test fly the aircraft.
The aircraft was flown, but that is an example of the interference with this operation. As I have tried to explain to the committee-and I think the minister agrees with me-the design, development and production of a new aircraft with new engines is an extremely difficult thing to do even if

you have a background of years and years of production experience, but to do that with a comparatively new plane of new design is very difficult indeed. To have the top brass of the air force and the Minister of National Defence sitting around and saying now, you had better take off because we have got to get back to Ottawa, would be an intolerable burden.
That is the sort of thing that has bedevilled the A. V. Roe Company ever since it has gone into production. They are producing a good aircraft. They have a good engine. It is tragic that they had to abandon the jet liner, but the reason there is disenchantment, as I said, with this concern is that when the prototype was developed the government said the prototype meant production. A prototype does not mean production. The development of a prototype may still mean that you are years away from production, and it is most unfortunate that this very valuable contribution to the Canadian aircraft industry has been so bedevilled by this sort of thing.
There is just one thing more, Mr. Chairman. When the first CF-100 was flown by the R.C.A.F. it was known that there were certain structural weaknesses in the aircraft, and exactly what they were. I have a memo here of what they were. Actually it was a spar web which had no real structural importance whatever in so far as the safety of the aircraft was concerned. When aircraft No. 18104 was delivered there were strict instructions on the aircraft not to fly it over a certain number of G's-I think it was three. Apparently it was flown and tested at 5J or even 6 G's. This internal spar web cracked because of the flexing of the main wing structure, not a serious difficulty. It did not make the aircraft unsafe in any way, and it was certainly a small defect which has now been remedied.
I state these things because I believe this firm has done a unique job, and a great deal of criticism has been levelled at A. V. Roe because of the government having said, We have these aircraft, when in fact they did not have them at all. That is one of the inherent dangers in this whole business of defence production.
My criticism of the department, Mr. Chairman, is simply this. We have the plants and we haye the technical know-how. What we do not have is a certain knowledge that, not the prototypes but the weapons which we need and which our allies need to defend the free world are going to begin rolling off the production lines. The representatives of the people of this country want to know the truth. We are prepared to be told the truth. If the time lag between the prototype of the aircraft and the production of that aircraft
Supply-Defence Production is two years, let us know it. Do not say that we have the best aircraft in the world and it will be in production next week or next month and we will be producing it at the rate of fifty aircraft a month, when anyone who knows about aircraft production knows that is impossible. Such a person disbelieves a great deal of the story-I think it is a good story-about what we are producing.
In the future-I do not say this particularly of the Minister of Defence Production, because I think he has been quite frank- let us not have these propaganda statements from the government that everything is perfect. Everything never can be perfect in defence production; it must be a continuous headache. Let us admit that. Let the Canadian people have the facts. Let us have our bottlenecks, and have them explained in this house. Let us have the whole story of defence production delivered to us in its brutal, unvarnished truth if that may be necessary. Let us not have these propaganda statements that we are producing the best aircraft in the world, when we merely have the prototype. Let us not have this propaganda that we have the finest minesweepers or the finest escort vessels when they are still on the stocks. Let us have the real facts. We are fooling no one but ourselves by pretending that our defence production is better than it is.

Mr. Chairman, in considering the estimates for defence production it is inevitable that the topic of decentralization of industry should come up. Today we have heard two hon. members refer to that subject. In looking at the report of the department, on page 26 we And some brief reference to the role played by the small industries division in defence production. It is largely on that topic I shall concentrate tonight.
Recently in the Financial Post an article appeared to the effect that small industry has lost interest in making its contribution to our defence production program. I wish to point out to the minister tonight, speaking as I do on behalf of a Manitoba constituency that has been eager and anxious to make a small contribution, that this article does not refer in any way to the Brandon situation. As a matter of fact the Brandon defence pool, which drew considerable attention just a little over a year ago, as a unique approach to the handling of the problem of industrial decentralization received honourable mention in the Financial Post. The example it established in pooling its industrial potential has since inspired other communities of similar size to follow suit.

Supply

Defence Production
Unfortunately, in the year's interval the head of the small industries division has changed, the personnel has changed, and it might be that the up-to-date situation is not completely known to those responsible. The Brandon pool is still active and is still vitally interested in using the capacity it possesses for production in connection with our defence program. This applies to Manitoba generally, too. It might be of interest to the members of this house to know that for the first time this year Manitoba is having a trade fair, modelled on the Canadian international trade fair, but of course on a considerably smaller scale. This fair is to be conducted in connection with the provincial exhibition which takes place annually in the city of Brandon. It is hoped that some 80 or 85 industrial exhibitors from Manitoba will make use of the space available. I refer to that fact merely to indicate that there is no justification for making the claim that small industries have lost their interest in making the most of the opportunities provided for industrial expansion during the present period of huge expenditures for defence purposes.
Reviewing the situation up to the present time, so far as the Brandon pool is concerned we have actually had very little success. I realize that the minister is sympathetic in his viewpoint toward this problem of feeding suitable contracts to small defence industries, but there are difficulties that have already been mentioned. For example, there is the difficulty of natural trends, where it is exceedingly hard to break industrial trends that are already under way. But I feel there have been instances when contracts might have been awarded to the small defence industries had the situation been completely known.
We have been fortunate in receiving a contract for the fabrication of steel by the Canadian Brown Steel Tank Company. Again, our oil refinery has received certain contracts with regard to the supplying of fuel. But one industry that we are nurturing carefully, the Melco Electric Company, as yet has not been favoured with a contract. Yet with its 65 employees it is ready and waiting, as the article in a recent issue of Saturday Night expressed the Manitoba viewpoint.
There is a particular problem on which I might get some information. The Oshkosh Filter & Softener Co. Canada Ltd. tendered on an item, No. G-39-3A-494. The tenders were first called in November, 1951, to supply a water softener plant for Camp Shilo. Inquiries I made early in March indicated that the contract had not been awarded, and there is still no information as to the present situation with regard to that particular job. I state the claim of this company because it is the

only water softener plant west of the great lakes; and it should be in good position to meet the requirements of the contract.
In an industrial situation such as that prevailing in my own constituency, the smaller industries are finding that the expense of submitting tenders is almost prohibitive. It would be a considerable source of encouragement if, from time to time, tangible results were forthcoming. Because of the slowness in getting the small industry division under way, owing to change of personnel and unforeseen difficulties, no doubt, one of the members of our Brandon pool hired an industrial consultant. Actually this was done, I believe, as a result of an inquiry I made last fall, one that has already been referred to by the hon. member for Queens, when I tried to get information as to the breakdown of defence production contracts on a provincial basis. In reply to that inquiry I received the information that such statistics were not available, mainly because industrial consultants had set up offices in the city of Ottawa and a great many of the contracts were being awarded through these agencies.
On learning of that fact, one of the companies involved in the Brandon pool hired the services of a consultant, but unfortunately this measure has not as yet overcome the difficulty. I re-emphasize the fact that any impression that was conveyed by the Financial Post article concerning lack of interest on the part of small defence industries certainly does not prevail in respect to our Brandon defence pool.
The subject of the difficulties faced in the process of the dispersal or decentralization of industry has been adequately covered by earlier speakers today. For example, we have already heard of the natural trend which has tended to plague our western countries, whereby we find that industrialization has become almost synonymous, with urbanization. The two processes are inseparable. Wherever you have industrialization, inevitably huge metropolitan areas establish themselves. That has been the tendency for the last century, at least in the western world.
I am not going to deal exhaustively tonight with the arguments pro or co.n as to the advantages or disadvantages of the process of urbanization; but social thinkers are rather inclined to emphasize the unsavoury social effects that follow in the wake of this process of urbanization. The whole matter was summed up neatly in an article, under the heading of "Modern Utopia" by Bruce Hutchison, which appeared in the Ottawa Citizen of February 19, 1952. He was referring to the situation in which the city of New York finds itself, and the typical New Yorkers

who are supposed to have the highest standard of living of any people in the world. Incidentally, it is a situation the city of Toronto is perhaps rapidly approaching as it is faced with the tremendous boom of the post-war period. Mr. Hutchison says:
. . . the rich New Yorker who is the envy of the entire world arises at about 6 a.m. and hurries through his breakfast. He is then driven some ten miles along slippery roads and through the heavy traffic of various towns to the nearest railway station.
Here he is jostled by the cranky morning crowds on a cold windswept and dirty railway platform while gigantic trains, half a mile long, flick by, at least one a minute. Finally his own train stops and he is swept inside by a stampede of angry commuters, all with a high standard of living, a stomach ulcer and a harassed look. One is lucky to get a seat on the train and sit there for an hour and ten minutes while it wallows into the Grand Central.
The Grand Central at about 9 a.m. presents a sight very much, I imagine, like the buffalo herds of the Canadian prairies before the white man arrived, except that these herds are in a greater hurry. Only an experienced half-back can buck this line.
But if one survives, this is by no means the end of the journey. Now the high standard man descends with swarms of his own kind down dark and unclean passages into the bowels of the earth where, out of a black tunnel, roars the subway train, pauses for half a minute with open doors and then, swallowing up its passengers as a whale swallows herring, is off again with deafening sound through the bored rock of Manhattan island.
Thus about two hours after leaving home the high standard man finally staggers into his office to begin work. At 5 p.m. he repeats the same process in reverse and after a quick bit of dinner collapses into bed to prepare himself for the same carefree life next day.
That is known as the highest standard of living in modern civilization.
We could go on at length dealing with the social problems that emerge as a result of the process of industrialization and urbanization. As I have already said, the hon, member for Queens dealt with that subject, indicating that around the central area of these huge metropoli you have problems of delinquency and the multiplicity of social evils that plague our society today. In order to break that trend toward urbanization conscious effort and planning is going to be required; and we have a whole new movement of community planning developing in our midst. But I maintain, Mr. Chairman, that the community planners can do nothing until such time as industry is dispersed or decentralized, because your population must inevitably gravitate in the direction of large industrial areas. I will admit that there is a natural process of decentralization developing. We find the movement toward suburbs becoming increasingly popular, mainly because of the social amenities deriving therefrom. But in this great country of ours, with the vast wide open spaces, there is no reason at all why
Supply-Defence Production industry could not be much more widely dispersed than it is at the present time.
I realize the problems of history. Industrial development got under way much earlier in the central provinces. There is the great geographical barrier, the great formidable natural barrier, the Pre-Cambrian shield, and so forth.
