But today, when resources are being discovered right across our country, resources which have been waiting for development up to the present time, there is every reason why encouragement should be given to this very necessary process of decentralization of industry.
Unfortunately, as much as we appreciate both the basic economic necessity and the military necessity of the St. Lawrence waterway, there is some criticism. The Minister of Transport, when speaking on this subject last December 6, said something along this line in regard to the criticism which was raised by the railroads, which were protesting that the construction of the St. Lawrence waterway would interfere with their business. In his reply the Minister of Transport referred to the industries that will grow up on the St. Lawrence waterway in such large numbers that they will offset any loss of business or revenue that might be suffered by the railways as a result of the construction of the canal. In other words, in the very near future we can contemplate the establishment of a Ruhr valley in eastern Canada, much longer and larger and more vulnerable than the original Ruhr valley; and those who had anything to do with the Ruhr valley during world war II will realize how vulnerable was that area, particularly to aerial attack. Once effective bombing tactics, techniques, methods and weapons were developed it was just a matter of time until almost the whole industrial potential of the Ruhr valley was destroyed, a factor which contributed largely to the successful conclusion of world war II.
This brings me to the point of the dictates of our military strategy and defence. The hon. member for Queens has already referred to this subject. If the international situation is as dangerous as indicated, of course every effort should be given to decentralize our strategic and vital industries over as wide an area as possible.
In addition to the necessity of overcoming natural trends and the demands of our defence requirements, I should like to pause for a brief moment and refer to the peculiar situation in which Canada finds herself. Decentralization of industry in Canada is a unique and difficult problem, different from the problem of dispersal of industry in other

Supply-Defence Production areas, mainly because of the factors I have already outlined, namely the historic factors and the factor, for example, that the west was opened up at a much later date than the eastern provinces. As a result we on the prairies now find ourselves in the situation industrially that prevailed in eastern Canada after world war I, when there was a great upsurge. We must admit-I am speaking now particularly from the point of view of Manitoba-that we have moved far from the basic agricultural economy. For example, we can boast of an industrial output last year of almost $600 million. Unfortunately most of that has been concentrated in the eastern area of our province, particularly around the city of Winnipeg. I think the actual figure is something like 85 per cent.
We also have a population problem. It is both a quantitative problem and a qualitative problem, the number of people we have and the kind of people we have. We have lost large numbers of our citizens. We have not even been able to maintain a population increase based on natural increase. We have been constantly going back. It is claimed, as I have pointed out before, that unfortunately it is the more enterprising citizen who moves to the industrial areas of the country; so we are handicapped both quantitatively and qualitatively. I repeat, Mr. Chairman, the situation is such in Canada that the opportunity is there. With huge expenditure for defence purposes we can help overcome these difficulties by a conscious, logical approach to the problem. I appreciate that the need is well recognized by the minister and those responsible for the handling of defence expenditures. I merely wish to emphasize that we are very interested in playing our part to the maximum, using the facilities we have, and at the same time enlarging those facilities during a period when every opportunity is there for industrial expansion.
One final word on this subject. It seems to me that a basic difficulty of democracy in Canada would be overcome, could we establish the ideal of an equitable distribution of industries across the country. We know that local democracy has lost some of its vitality and some of its enthusiasm mainly because our communities have been depopulated with the constant drain of our human resources arising from rural urban migration. By relocating or encouraging smaller industry in some of these smaller communities we can assist measurably in re-establishing and reactivating the spirit of democracy in our local communities. I say that we cannot have a vital democracy on other

levels of government, either provincial or federal, unless the individual citizen in his home community is carrying the responsibility of local affairs.
What could result from the establishment of one small industry has been very nicely indicated by F. J. Lyle, who is the director of the trade and industry branch of the Ontario government.
He said:
A Canadian plant employing 150 men entails, on the average, these material benefits:
Support for one 22-room school and its teachers;
110 occupied homes;
A livelihood for 24 professional men;
Purchase and operation of 135 automobiles and services for them;
33 retail salespeople and annual sales of $325,000;
Support for 6,600 farm acres whose products are consumed by the factory employees, their families, and the families of those tradesmen and others who are sustained by the factory.
That demonstrates dramatically the beneficial effects that will result and are resulting as this process of decentralization continues. I only hope that every effort will be made to carry out the intentions of the small industries division, as expressed at page 26 of the report.
Then I would submit one final question to the minister, and this on a different subject. I noted that in his review of the activities of the department he made reference to the manufacture of -5 calibre machine guns, and also the ammunition for the machine guns. I believe the factory carrying out that contract is known as Canadian Arsenals. Several times in the house I have made inquiries as to the status of -5 calibre armament. I know the subject is discussed repeatedly in military circles. I first became aware of the controversy during world war II when the tendency was to emphasize larger armament for the Royal Canadian Air Force. For example, during the progress of world war II we moved from -303 machine guns, finally concentrating on 20 millimetre cannons. The controversy then, as it is today, was between the United States and Britain as to the respective merits of the -5 machine gun and the 20 millimetre cannon.
Repeatedly the effectiveness of the -5 weapon is questioned by those in authority. Some few weeks ago I made reference to the comments of a pilot in the 410th squadron located in England, the comments of Major Davies of the United States air force, one of the United States aces fighting in Korea, and more recently to the comments of Dr.
G.	M. Shrum, a member of Canada's national defence board and of the national research council.

Dealing with the presence of obsolete and obsolescent weapons in our forces, he had this to say in regard to the -5 machine gun:
Jet planes, travelling at 700 miles an hour, are using obsolete machine guns.
"They might as well be shooting at each other with pea shooters."
That is language similar to that used by the pilot in the 410th squadron overseas.
The question that arises out of these comments in this: Are we embarking upon a large-scale production of -5 calibre machine guns and armaments, which many people feel is obsolescent? If it is effective at all today, it is obsolescent and very soon will be superseded by rocket projectiles still in the experimental stage.

Mr. Chairman, I believe our defence efforts would fall under three headings. First there is the planning stage; then there is the provision of personnel and, third, the provision of equipment for those personnel. I think all hon, members in the committee are familiar with the details of the planning stage. It is built up on a three year program in order to meet our commitments for the defence of Canada, our commitments in connection with the North Atlantic Treaty Organization and the United Nations, and to build up a general strategic reserve. That is based upon a three-year plan. I think it is essential that all hon. members realize that we are working on such a plan.
With regard to personnel, we have had many assurances from the Minister of National Defence that the provision of personnel is moving along satisfactorily, according to plan. Figures published in tonight's newspaper, if correct, would give assurance along those lines. The official figures as stated in that newspaper indicate that in the active component of the Royal Canadian Navy there are 14,000 men, in the active army some
50.000	men and in the active air force some 33,000, making a total of about 97,000 men. This is within an appreciable distance of the target set for the number of personnel required at the end of the three-year period.
Figures are also given regarding the reserve forces, the navy having 7,000, the army
44.000	and the air force 6,000. We have no target figure at which those reserve forces are aiming; but I should like to call attention to various statements made recently by such commanders as General Eisenhower, stressing the importance of building up the reserve forces to a point where in due course they would be ready and available to take their place with the more active components of the armed forces of the various nations, should the world situation deteriorate.
Supply-Defence Production
I think it is fair to say that the general manpower situation in the armed forces, according to the target set two years ago by the Minister of National Defence, appears to be in a satisfactory state.
Now we come to the question of equipment which, I believe, is provided by the Department of Defence Production. I do not think it is the responsibility of that department to indicate design or even the number of various types of ships, aircraft or guns required. If my interpretation of the responsibilities of the department is correct, then it is the responsibility of the department to produce the weapons and equipment which the Department of National Defence indicates are necessary for our defence effort. Of course there are bound to be consultations. No doubt the Minister of Defence Production might on occasions point out that certain equipment could not be provided, and that it was not possible for this country to produce certain types. All in all it is the responsibility of the minister to produce the equipment which the defence department requires. I am not going to presume to tell the minister how to do it because I do not think there is a man on the government benches who is better able to carry out these duties than the present minister.
What I want to know is, how is that getting along? Is there a backlog? Has the Department of National Defence asked for any equipment or materials which the minister has not been able to supply? Is he marching side by side in the production of equipment with the department which is responsible for producing the manpower? I think that is the question, in simple terms, which the people of Canada want answered.
I do not think that we can hold the minister responsible for producing this or that type of weapon. Whether the weapon he is asked to produce is obsolete or is a new model is for the Department of National Defence to decide. What I would like to obtain from the minister when he replies is a simple, straightforward statement as to how his department is meeting the demands which have been made upon it by the Department of National Defence.
Has he been able to keep pace with the intake of men, in so far as the navy is concerned? Has he been able to produce a sufficient number of vessels so the personnel which joins the Royal Canadian Navy will be able to take their training and if necessary go to sea in vessels which are now available? Or will they have to wait for another six or twelve months before vessels are available?
As far as the army is concerned, have the active components of the army now serving in

Supply-Defence Production Korea and Europe adequate equipment according to the standards which were laid down by the Department of National Defence? Or is the minister still trying in some respects to obtain equipment in order to come up to the standards required?
In so far as the Royal Canadian Air Force is concerned, we know that the number of personnel to meet the final target are not yet available, but we have had assurances from the Minister of National Defence that they will be available by the target date. Well and good; but will there be aircraft which those personnel will require available when needed?
What we want is just a simple, straightforward statement. I do not think the actual number of guns or the number of suits of clothing mean anything to us. Just tell us whether the department is keeping up to the requests which are made to it, or give us a frank statement that in some respects it is falling down.
Supposing the situation does deteriorate; supposing this period of cold war should deteriorate into active warfare, in what position is this country to speed up vital production in its general armament industry? From the stress laid upon it by commanders of the United Nations forces, by our own Minister of National Defence and by commanders in this country, we know that considerable importance is placed upon our reserve forces. We cannot expect them to be fully equipped at this time. Nobody would expect that, but we would like to know what reasonable chance there is for this reserve force to be fully equipped within a reasonable period after the situation becomes so obvious that we have to start building up the general strategic reserve of the United Nations which we may be called upon to supply.
What is the position regarding the possibility of swinging into full production of war materials? I am not going to ask whether the reserve army is fully equipped, because I know the answer. Of course it is not; you do not expect it to be. What I do want to know is this. Is the machinery there so that on comparatively short notice we can swing into full production? As I say, if the minister can give us a simple, straightforward picture of the general situation I believe it will answer the queries which are in the minds of a great many people who are giving serious thought to this situation at the present time.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Mr. Chairman-

Mr. Chairman, I take it that we are in committee and the minister is answering.
[Mr. PearkesJ

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I am awfully tired of listening. My hon. friend has been speaking for most of the evening, and perhaps he will give way. I shall start with the last question and work backward to the questions asked by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra.
The hon. member who has just spoken is well aware of the nature of war production. When you are depending on mass production there is a long tooling process and then tremendous output. We are following that path deliberately so that if the worst comes to the worst and we have to fight a war we will have the productive capacity. We would have far more production than we can use in this country under present circumstances. I remember one occasion during the last war, I think it was in 1944, when there was a shipping delay lasting about six weeks. The U-boats were active and very few boats were loaded. In those six weeks we had the railroad line from Windsor to Montreal, as well as several branch lines, piled high with munitions of war on their way overseas. That is the way production rolls when you really get going.
My hon. friend asked if the manpower of the three services were adequately supported with equipment. I believe the answer is yes, although I will admit at once that part of that equipment is from the last war. But in the case of aircraft, the production of F-86 aircraft, which is the principal plane of aggression, is well ahead of schedule. Apparently the Royal Canadian Air Force are satisfied with the production because they have diverted about sixty planes to our allies. Those planes are now in Korea, planes that we thought were to equip the Canadian air force. We are turning out the F-86 as fast as the R.C.A.F. can use them. If more are needed we can step up production, particularly when the Orenda engine comes into production in increasing quantities.
The CF-100 is intended as a defensive plane for this country. It is a long-range, allweather fighter, particularly adapted to use in Canada. While three squadrons of these planes will eventually go overseas, I do not think any unit is waiting for these particular planes at this time.
Then with regard to ships, all the ships of the last war have been or are being activated. I am quite sure that all naval personnel are able to train on modern ships. The new escort vessel is a very complicated ship. I might say that the weapons of today are about ten times as complicated as the weapons of the last war. However, the escort program is coming along. Unfortunately in the newer equipment one piece is usually not invented and that is holding

up completion of the whole on some occasions; nevertheless I believe the answer to the hon. member for Nanaimo is yes. The program is meeting the requirements of the Canadian services at the present time.
We must keep in mind that the supply lines in Korea are American and the supply lines in Europe are British, so we are not shipping ordinary supplies to the front. Ammunition and supplies of food and clothing are not going from Canada to the front. We would be quite able to supply them if that were the situation, but it happens that the line of supply has been organized differently. I repeat that I think we can say that every member of the armed services, whether in Canada or abroad, is properly equipped with modern weapons.
Perhaps I might say a word about dispersal of industry. Dispersal is an easy thing to talk about and somewhat hard to arrange, and I think there are some rather weird ideas about it. We should remember that we have a three-year program. It may be very fine to set up a substantial industry in a small town remote from industrial areas, equip that factory to produce for three years, and then presumably close it down. My hon. friend mentioned the A. V. Roe plant. He said it would be a wonderful industry for a small city. May I point out that the A. V. Roe plant today employs
10,000	people and shortly will employ 18,000. If you put that plant in a small city, what does the city do? The city must first build houses for 10,000 families. They must build schools to service the houses and they must have water supplies and sewage disposal plants to correspond. That may be a good thing to do to a small town but I would not like to be guilty of perpetrating that sort of thing.
I recall that in the last war experts made a very careful examination, of where to put an explosives plant which was going to involve about $15 million in construction. The report came back that they thought the ideal place for it would be in Port Arthur. I said, "Take another look. It is going somewhere, but it is not going anywhere near Port Arthur." We like to run an economy in Port Arthur that remains fairly stable from year to year. To put a plant of that kind, with the employment it would require, into a city the size of Port Arthur would be a crime against the economics of the whole district. Therefore the explosives plant was put in the vicinity of a much larger city. When the war was over it was dismantled and the several thousand employees who had worked there were absorbed into the general industry of the city. That is somewhat illustrative. I may
Supply-Defence Production say that it went to Winnipeg. My hon. friend will remember that.
I remember that.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: You handled it fairly well. I passed it on to my hon. friend. I was generous. That is the story of dispersal. Take the city of Brandon,. I think it would be wrong to put an industry employing 2,000 people in Brandon, operate it for two years and then close it. What in the world would they do with the houses they had built to house these people?
For a small industry?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
It would have to be in proportion to the area; but in mass production for war, industries are not small. I took a little time after dinner and prepared a statement showing the difficulty of meeting the frequent requests for allocating war production between provinces. A question has been raised as to why we do not publish figures showing the value of projects placed in the various provinces. The simple answer, which I have given on several occasions, is that we see no value in giving such figures inasmuch as they in no way reflect the impact of the defence program on the various sectors of the country. They do not take into account the large proportion of subcontracting which is inherent in this type of work. They make no allowance for the source of raw materials going into the contracts, and in many cases they are misleading because contracts placed at head offices in Ottawa or Montreal are often carried out in company plants which may be located as far away as the east coast or the west coast.
Let me assure hon. members that I am as interested as they are in ensuring that industry in every part of Canada has an opportunity to play its fair share in this over-all program. I fully recognize the arguments that are put forward concerning the desirability of locating our defence potential in such a way as to minimize the dangers of attack. Nevertheless it is one thing to express this pious wish and it is another thing to implement a policy. I think the only proper way of examining the situation is to look at a few of the major programs.
Let us first look at aircraft. There are three major prime contractors in this field, Canadair, A. V. Roe and de Havilland. These three companies will be responsible for about a billion 'dollars worth of defence contracts, and if we allocated contracts we would allocate about half of that to the province of Quebec and half to the province of Ontario. But what are the facts? Ther are nine other

Supply-Defence Production firms with substantial overhaul and modification contracts, one in Halifax, two in Winnipeg, one in Edmonton, and one in Vancouver. Furthermore, the percentage of subcontracts in this field is extremely heavy. A. V. Roe, for example, has 15 major subcontractors and over 600 important suppliers. Many of these subcontractors and suppliers are in part located outside the province of Ontario.
Then let us take shipbuilding. The major contracts have been placed at Halifax, Saint John, Lauzon, Sorel, Montreal, Kingston, Port Arthur, Vancouver and Victoria, whereas smaller contracts have been placed at such centres as Charlottetown, P.E.I. and Trenton, Pictou, Lunenburg and Liverpool, Nova Scotia. There again these shipyards subcontract all across the country. We find factories on the prairies building components to go into these shipyards.
Taking the automotive field, major contracts naturally are located at Windsor and Oshawa. However, several smaller contracts for specialized equipment have been placed in Montreal, St. Claire and Valcourt, P.Q., at St. Catharines and Hamilton in Ontario, and at Winnipeg, Manitoba.
With respect to weapons, major artillery contracts have been placed at Sorel and small arms contracts with Canadian Arsenals, the work being done at their Long Branch plant. Other contracts have been placed with Dominion Bridge. A considerable amount of its work is being done at their Burnaby, B.C., branch, and by Firestone Tire and Rubber, Hamilton, Turnbull Elevator, Toronto, and
H.	and R. Arms, Drummondville. Here again these plants are focal centres for subcontracting. We have no method of segregating the impact of the subcontracting from these plants. I know that Sorel Industries are subcontracting a good deal of their work outside the province of Quebec.
Turning to ammunition, all major contracts have been placed with Canadian Arsenals at Ottawa, but 80 per cent of the work is being done at St. Paul l'Ermite and Quebec city, and 20 per cent at Lindsay, Ontario. Important subcontracts have been placed with Trenton Steel in Nova Scotia, a number of Montreal firms, Sorel Industries, small firms located around Quebec city, and firms in the Toronto area such as Graham Bell Enameling, Streetsville, T. W. Hand, Cooks-ville, United Steel Corporation, Welland, Wallaceburg Brass of Wallaceburg, and Orillia Sheet Metal, Orillia.
The torpedo program will be extensively subcontracted. The torpedo body will probably be built in British Columbia.

In electronics, the main program will be located in the Toronto, Hamilton, Belleville and Montreal areas, where the big four of the industry are located. However, there are important contracts at Cossor Limited, Halifax, and subcontracts in such places as Quebec city, Drummondville, Windsor, London and Brantford, Ontario.
I turn now to clothing and equipage. This is a very complicated program to analyse from the angle of geographical distribution, because of the prevalence of multiple branch plants. For example, Canadian Cottons receives orders which are credited to its Montreal head office, whereas the mills are located in Ontario and New Brunswick.
In fuels and lubricants, the prime contracts have a geographical distribution related to the location of defence installations and their usage of such items as gasoline, etc. However, the flow of supplies creates a considerable indirect effect on producing areas such as Alberta, which is not reflected in the provincial placing of prime contracts.
With regard to food the same principle applies. Food tends to be bought locally, but may have much of its origin in areas such as the prairie region.
From these few remarks you will note that, although there are definite limitations as to the geographical distribution that can be achieved, the program is indeed having an impact on the whole of Canada, from coast to coast. I have mentioned a large number of small towns that are doing defence work as a result of subcontracts, and these examples could be multiplied many times over. This statement shows the impossibility of trying to analyse contracts by geographical boundaries. All we record is the prime contractor, and his address may mean nothing at all so far as the impact of his contract is concerned.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra has regretted that there was no long-term plan for this department, and that it was staffed with officers borrowed from industry who were obviously not permanent officers. It was organized as a temporary department. As I say, the program was the three-year NATO program, joined in by all the free nations. We hope that after the program is completed, and after the production facilities have been established, the maintenance of a separate department will not be necessary. After the last war the department of munitions and supply was merged with the Department of Trade and Commerce. I hope that in due course this department can be merged with an existing department.
The reason we have borrowed men from industry is that you are able to borrow men

you could not possibly hire. We have no compunction about asking an industry to lend us its top executive for a period of time. We go to companies like Bell Telephone, Steel Company of Canada, Ford or General Motors and say we want so and so. Sometimes we have a bit of an argument, but in my experience extending over the last ten years or more no company has definitely refused to lend us the man we said we wanted. These men are paid rather better than civil servants for the main part, and therefore we say to the company that we are sorry we cannot pay the salary but we will pay his living expenses and you pay his salary. In every case, I believe, the company has agreed to that procedure. I may say that no department of government has ever been better served than has the department for which I have been responsible, as a result of borrowing men from industry for temporary jobs.
Then there was the matter of the distribution of defence orders placed outside of Canada, which was mentioned by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra. It was a major policy decision that, in view of the threat of communism, it seemed obvious that if a last ditch stand had to be made it would have to be made in the defence of North America. If the great world struggle between the two different ideologies should actually occur, it seemed to the government it would be the duty of this country to prepare for that last ditch stand. We decided, therefore, to standardize weapons with the United States, our next door neighbour. This policy called for a different type of weapon than we used in the last war. However, the type would have been different whatever the country with whom we standardized.
I think the fact that we have standardized on United States army weapons has in no way handicapped the program. There was a departure in that we adopted the Centurion tank of Great Britain instead of the United States Sherman tank. The reason for that was that both tanks were operating in the same area, and for the type of warfare presently in progress the Centurion tank seemed to be doing at least as well as the Sherman tank. I believe the government of the United States has also purchased Centurion tanks, perhaps for the same reason we did.
Then we have been urged to further expand the steel industry. We did undertake a tremendous expansion three years ago, and then it came somewhat later than I had hoped. I had tried to bring about some expansion two years earlier; however the commencement of the expansion was undertaken about two years ago. The expansion program
Supply-Defence Production when completed will result in adding about one-third to the present productive capacity of our steel industry. This expansion has been carried out with private funds, and will come into production partly in the fourth quarter of this year and the balance early next year. When we have that additional capacity, Canada will be more nearly self-supporting in steel. We never have been entirely self-supporting, and I presume that imports will be required even with the increased expansion.
The hon. member referred to the lack of a steel industry on the west coast.
West of the great lakes.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: West of the great lakes there are two or three. There is one at Winnipeg, one at Calgary and one at Vancouver.
But just scrap metal plants.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I know, but the fourth largest steel industry in this country survived on scrap metal from its founding about thirty-five years ago up until one year ago. It never used anything else. It did so because scrap metal was available to meet the requirements of a very large mill, Dominion Foundry and Steel. I see no purpose in the west coast going into the primary steel business, as long as the west coast supplies sufficient scrap to keep the local industry going. To me the logical development would be to expand the production of finished steel, and when the time comes that the supply of scrap is not adequate then to add a blast furnace, which is exactly what Dofasco has done within the last year or two. I have said before that the opening of the steel deposits there is the logical procedure for blast furnaces.
The iron deposits.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
If British Columbia is going to miss the few thousand tons of iron ore that will be shipped from there until the blast furnace is built, the deposits are hardly sufficient to warrant a steel industry in any event. All I can say is that the government will be prepared to extend to the steel industry in British Columbia any help that it is extending or has extended to the steel industry in eastern Canada.
I think that covers the questions which were asked.

There were two other points that I raised, Mr. Chairman. One had to do with the extraordinary powers given under the Defence Production Act, particularly the power to seize an industry. The other had to do with the building of modern merchant vessels.
2780	HOUSE OF
Supply-Defence Production Mr. Howe: The powers were taken when the country was much more alarmed than it seems to be at the moment, though I doubt whether the situation was more threatening then than it is today. The powers were taken in view of the possibility that there might be all-out war within a very few months. The important feature is not the powers the government has; it is the powers the government uses. We have used the powers to control prices. We have been keeping a control on materials where the war requirements created shortages that would have an effect on prices. For instance, no steel price can be increased without previous advice to and approval of the government. The domestic price of all metals requires prior approval of the government. The same thing is true with regard to most of the raw materials that are being bought for the defence program. We have not passed laws but the controller, clothed with authority, has instructed the trade that this procedure must be followed; and it has been followed. I see no reason to cancel those powers today.
If I may interrupt the minister, may I point out that I did not refer to those powers particularly. I referred to the power to seize an industry.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The powers to seize an industry are the powers to prevent a contractor of the government from getting into a position in which he cannot carry out his contract. That authority is not an unusual provision in any contract. Every construction contract that is written by the government or by anybody else provides that if the contractor gets into difficulty, the owner can take over his equipment and finish the job at his expense. That is an ordinary provision.
But not take over his business?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes; take over his business, as a rule. His business has got to be good for the completion of the contract.
That is done only through court procedure.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Our provision does not provide for taking over a business if a contractor has a defence contract in one plant and is doing other business in other plants; there is no provision that allows us to take over his entire business. We take over the plant which is carrying out the war contract, and we operate that plant until we obtain our deliveries. We did that several times in the last war.
I accept the point of view that we incur liabilities by so doing. If by putting in a controller we made the situation worse instead of better, we would be responsible to the


owner for damages. I have always felt sure of that. But fortunately all the situations worked out well. The situation never arose where we turned back a plant in worse condition than when we took it over. I see nothing dangerous in the power the government takes to protect the production which is essential to its defence program or its war program. That is the only power for seizing property that the government has under the emergency regulations.
The minister means under the Defence Production Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes; under the Defence Production Act.
Since the war has any occasion arisen when it was necessary to seize a business or part of it?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No, not at all; but there must have been ten or fifteen occasions during the second world war.
During the war?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes. As to merchant ships, may I say that the merchant ships seem to be adequate to meet emergency conditions. Shipping is fairly easy at the moment. Ninety-five per cent of the ships afloat that carry bulk cargoes are of the same type as the ships that make up Canada's bulk cargo fleet. In the allocation of naval duties by NATO, Canada was allocated the task of escorting ships on the north Atlantic. We are preparing to do that job. In the program of building escort vessels I see nothing which carries with it the thought that we should have a complementary program of building fast merchant ships. We are guarding the ships of all nations, not simply the ships of the merchant marine.

The minister has told us that we have tooled up beyond our immediate needs, a wise and reasonable precaution. Can he tell us just what is happening to this extra productive capacity? Is it on a care and maintenance basis, or who is responsible for seeing that it is kept in top condition?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
It will mean that as it comes into production the goods actually on order will be produced in a very short time. That has not happened yet. Then the plants will be kept on a care and maintenance basis and returned to other purposes. The productive capacity will be there. For instance, at Canadair we will be turning out aircraft, I suppose, at the rate of 50 a month. My hon. friend knows that after we have in hand our supplies for the current situation, the requirements may be 10 aircraft a month

simply in order to make up wastage. Nevertheless we have the large capacity in case war comes. It is a weapon which I think is more valuable than are aircraft already produced and on the ground.
There is no chance of this extra productive capacity being sold if the emergency fades away?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No.

I also wish to ask one or two questions of the minister. I have been greatly interested in the statement he has given us and in this report of the defence production department. It is, of course, clear that up to the present time we have no details of any kind which enable us to arrive at any judgment of our own. We merely have the interesting statement from the minister and the interesting report.
As has been pointed out already, actually the estimates of the Department of Defence Production are in one way misleading because of the small amount actually they involve. We have $7 million for ordinary administration, to which I will come back later. One large item is to provide capital assistance for the construction, acquisition, extension or improvement of capital equipment or works. I take it that is pursuant to the duty laid on the department, as set out at page 9 of the report from which I quote:
... to "examine into, organize, mobilize and conserve the resources of Canada contributory to, and the sources of supply of, defence supplies".
What I want to ask the minister is this. I put this forward with an open mind because I do not want to make a request which is unreasonable. On the other hand I feel that we in the opposition ought to have some direct evidence beyond what we have at the moment. What I suggest to the minister, at any rate as a beginning, is that we should be informed of, or be allowed to see, the contracts or at any rate the large ones covering this $85 million investment. That is an investment which is rather different from the others because it is one to provide for construction and so on. It is really an investment which we ourselves make as a nation in production.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I just want to say I would be delighted to furnish that material if we could get to the items. I do not think I can furnish the material on the discussion on general administration.

Do I understand the minister to say that he thinks I am anticipating my questions, and that they should come at a later stage?
Supply-Defence Production

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes.

I will accept that and go on to the other thing I was going to say.
What is the relationship between defence production and national defence in this respect? I realize that it is up to national defence to originate its own orders and to pass them on to defence production; nevertheless defence production has a very considerable staff of able experts in the contract business. My question is this. When a request for material comes from national defence to defence production, is it acted upon automatically? Is any scrutiny given to it? I mention this because one or two cases have arisen, one of which was manifestly ridiculous. There were small amounts involved, but when you touch a soft spot you wonder whether there are others. Does the defence production department accept this automatically, or do they bring their trained common sense to bear on it and if they find anything that looks as if it is out of line will they criticize it?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The duty of the Department of Defence Production is to be the servant of the armed services. It is the duty of the armed services to say what they want, write *the specifications, draw the plans and say how many. If the requisition comes signed by the minister of the department, or in certain cases by his deputy minister, accompanied by a certificate of encumbrance which provides the funds with which to buy it, it is the duty of defence production to provide it. In other words if the army decides they want a gold-plated piano, and they send along a requisition accompanied by a certificate of encumbrance, we buy the gold-plated piano. If it is a nickel-plated piano we can object, because nickel is a scarce commodity. But as to a gold-plated one, we have no reason to object; we would go and buy it. An impossible situation would arise if the Department of Defence Production challenged the right of the armed services to buy what they said they needed, and for which they provide the financial encumbrance.
But they cannot say whom to buy it from.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
No, they cannot say that; that is the business of defence production. They can say what they want, but whether it is procured by production within the country, or whether it is bought from without, that is a decision entirely for the Department of Defence Production. However, if there is something peculiar about the order it is reported to me. In a different capacity, as a member of the government of Canada, I can

Supply-Defence Production consult with my colleague, the Minister of National Defence, who is also a member of the government of Canada and draw it to his attention, which I do. If he looks at the matter and says: "No, the order is correct", that ends it.
There are two or three questions I should like to ask the minister. Is it the intention of the government that the Department of Defence Production should go out of existence in 1954?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Oh, no; it will go out of existence when the administration can be carried out in more economical form. The point was that the department of munitions and supply, when maintaining a skeleton of the department which was flung all the way across the country, was a more expensive way of buying, carrying out the requirements of the defence services, than to combine with another department which had offices in various parts of Canada. Of course we cannot foresee these matters, but I would say the present department would be wound up when its work had diminished to the point that the overhead of the department was not warranted.

The minister said that upon the expiration of the three-year program he thought the Department of Defence Production would no longer be required. That would be in the year 1954. I was surprised at that because I had-

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: We cannot be wound up that fast.

No. I thought that once this three-year program is completed, then the NATO countries would almost of necessity have to carry on with a further program of some type; that they simply would not be able to say; "we have prepared a certain amount of equipment, and we have set up certain manufacturing facilities. Now we can go back to normal times and let the matter stand". I should think the probability is there will be another program following the completion of this three-year program. Is that so?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The present act expires in 1956. The situation will be reviewed. I do not know what is going to follow the present program. We do not plan programs. That is a matter for the services.
Another question had to do with the defence purchasing done by the department for other countries. The minister said nothing about that today. Can he tell us the situation in that regard?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The Canadian Commercial Corporation, associated with the department, acts for other governments. I said today we had placed something over $250 million worth of contracts for the government of the United States. We place certain orders for the United Kingdom and for the other countries, but not on a large scale. Any foreign requirements that are placed in Canada through the government. are placed toy the Canadian Commercial Corporation, through the department, in turn.
Would it be possible to get those figures for "the other countries"?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No, I would not like to give them; I do not think it would be appropriate.

To what extent is the department in the operation of facilities? For example, mines. I know that it is operating, or has some operating agreement in connection with the Emerald mine in southeastern British Columbia.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes.
Are there any other instances of that kind?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No, I think that is the only mine we own. Of course we are in the mining business in uranium in a big way, but I think the only new mining venture is the mine the hon. member spoke of, Emerald tungsten. It is doing very well, I might say, financially and otherwise.

Yes. I believe it has turned out to be quite profitable. I understand that it is operated under a management contract with a private mining company; in other words, the department is not actually conducting mining operations.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No; we have an engineer on the job, but the actual operating is done by a private company.

One other question on the item. There is an increase in the vote of over $1,300,000. Actually what was spent during the last fiscal year was an estimated sum of $5,158,000. Why is there that increase; what is the main reason?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Larger expenditure, larger staff. The staff has been extended to take on additional responsibility.
I should like to ask one question on subcontracts. Does the subcontractor come under the defence production management? Does he deal directly with the minister's office as a subcontractor?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No; he reports to the main contractor, but the Department of Defence Production reserves the right to approve the subcontractor. We do not deal directly with him; we deal with him through the main contractor.
You approve of him doing the work, though?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes, we have that right.

I should like to know a little more about the staff. I did not realize the numbers were so large. There must be a good many hundred people indicated at pages 154 and 155. Would the minister say something about the size of the staff and, in particular, I should like to know what he does with about 20 economists. I did not realize so many were needed to give these orders.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: We have about 1,700 people on the staff.
It says there are 1,900.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes, 1,900. I believe the book rather than my memory.
So would I.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Then, of course, we have inspectors on every construction job going on across the country, and those in the field staff of the general purchasing branch, which is charged against departmental administration.
How many of these 1,900 came from previously existing departments?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: About 800. Some 650 were absorbed from Canadian Commercial Corporation and 150 from the Department of Trade and Commerce.
Then will the minister tell me about all these economists?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The economists are really statisticians. To keep track of programs of this kind we must have men who are responsible for analysing figures, and keeping the programs in order.

Could the minister say
whether Canadian Arsenals Limited is going into large-scale production of -5 ammunition?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
There is a considerable program of -5 aircraft guns, partly for Canadian requirements and partly for NATO requirements. It is a combined order for two or three countries.
Supply-Defence Production
Is there any information about tender No. G-39-3A-494 for the installation of a water softening plant at Camp Shilo?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I have heard vaguely about that-something about the process. However, I am asking that the information be looked up. I know the order has not been passed yet, but just why I am not sure.

Has the
minister received any request from the government of Newfoundland for defence orders for any of the government plants down there?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The only one I remember is from the new MIAG plant. It is a machinery plant, and I believe the products to be produced at the plant are being exhibited at the trade fair. The plant is not yet in production.

It is not
yet constructed.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Sample machines are being shown at the fair, and I am sure our manufacturers will be interested in seeing them. After that I should hope that further orders will be placed.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
80. To provide capital assistance for the construction. acquisition, extension or improvement of capital equipment or works by private contractors engaged in defence contracts, or by crown plants operated on a management-fee basis, or by crown companies under direction of the Minister of Defence Production, subject to the approval of treasury board, $85,000,000.
I take it this is the item to which the minister referred when he asked me to reserve my question until later.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: This is the capital assistance item. In 1951-52, out of an appropriation of $100 million, only $46,165,000 was expended,
Is that out of a vote of $100 million?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Yes, out of a vote of $100 million. This year the vote is $85 million, which includes a carry-over of $66 million from last year. That is allocated as follows: Canadian General Electric, $970,000; Canadian Steel Improvements, $1,718,000; Cockshutt Aircraft Limited, $797,000; Dominion Engineering Limited, $1,473,000; John Inglis Company Limited, $5,810,000; Light Alloys Limited, $50,000; Peacock Brothers, $1,188,000; A. V. Roe, the jet engine plant, $16,176,000; Rotax of Canada Limited, $2,496,000; Sperry Gyroscope, $1,618,000; the crown company, Canadian Arsenals Limited, $8,800,000; and to

Supply-Defence Production provide miscellaneous private contractors with government machinery installed in private plants, $43,665,000.
How does the minister suggest that we should get a further understanding of this? There is no security involved in these contracts, is there? Could they not be filed?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Yes, but I think the proper place to file them is in the committee on defence expenditures. I would not like to lay them on the table of the house, because that would not be the proper procedure. However, my officers would be glad to attend before the committee on defence expenditures and produce any of the contracts in which the hon. member may be interested.
I might add that all the contracts involve complete government ownership. If a building is built, it is built on land owned by the crown, and the buildings belong to the crown. If it is machinery, the machinery is the property of the crown and remains the property of the crown. I might say from the experience of the last war that the salvage was around 40 per cent of the original value of the buildings or machines.

The minister says there is no objection to the production of these contracts before the committee on defence expenditures. However, he does not wish to file them here. Is there any real difference? In both cases they are made public, are they not?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes; but in one case they are simply dumped on the table, while in the other they are laid on the table by an officer of the department who can answer questions about them. I might say, so far as tabling in the house is concerned, that all these contracts develop out of orders in council tabled in the house. If the hon. member cares to look through the records he will find orders in council covering each of these capital expenditures.
Is it possible to have further details about this $43 million, which is nearly half the amount?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes. The hon. member can have details of every machine that has been bought. It has been machinery installed in private plants. We have complete records, and will be glad to produce those records for every machine installed.
It constitutes over half the total vote. Would it be possible to have a list of the firms?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: It would be a large volume, out it is available. We would be very pleased to give it.
How many firms are involved, approximately?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Many plants with defence contracts have government-owned machinery installed in them. There are probably two or three hundred of them.
The government would purchase certain of this machinery outright?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes.

And this vote is for that
purpose?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes.

The minister said that last year $46 million was spent. The figures at page 156 show that up to January 31,	1952,
$13,561,757 had been spent, and the figure estimated for the balance of the year is $16,334,356, making an estimated total for the last fiscal year of $29,896,113. How did the figure increase from $29 million to $46 million?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The original procedure was that capital assistance was provided from the vote of the Department of National Defence. There is a combination of two sources of funds, so far as last year's capital assistance is concerned. This year it is all in the Department of Defence Production. The books simply show expenditures from the Department of Defence Production. In addition, certain capital assistance was arranged through the Department of National Defence.
Apparently the estimate last year carried under the Department of Defence Production-

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes.
-was $100 million?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: And also $50 million in the Department of National Defence.
The real situation is that taking the two votes together, the total appropriation for this purpose was $150 million, with the expenditure being $46 million; is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes.
This year the vote is to be $85 million, or is there another sum being voted for the Department of National Defence?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No, it is all in this.
So it will really be $85 million as against $150 million; is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That is right.

I want to be clear as to what the minister is going to do in the way of filing contracts. I understand the minister is going to make them available to the defence expenditures committee, which by the way will meet again on Tuesday. I think they ought to be available to us before these estimates are finally passed because this is our only chance to ask the minister questions regarding them. Can it be understood that we will get them in time to study them before these estimates are finally passed?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Every order in council providing for an expenditure has been tabled. If my hon. friend will have his assistant go through the records of the house he will find every one. I do not think we should be asked to table them twice.

I am interested in what the minister says. It may be that he is correct in saying the orders in council cover everything, but does he mean that the contracts are embodied in the orders in council or merely that the orders in council authorize the making of the contracts?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Authorize the making of the contracts.

I should like to go back to what the minister said, that he would table these contracts-that is what I think he said, and that is what I want- with the defence expenditures committee. I am asking now whether that can be done on Tuesday, which is their first meeting. I come back to my request that I think we should have these and study them before this item is finally passed. I think the minister will agree that that is reasonable.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I am not a member of the defence expenditures committee. I understand that the chairman of the steering committee has planned a program for next Tuesday. Witnesses are to be there. We have appropriate witnesses. For instance, if we have a witness on guns he will be pleased to file details of capital expenditures for the gun program. I would point out that the orders in council are very complete; they show the entire bases of the contracts. They have been tabled in this house. I cannot read them to my hon. friend personally; nevertheless if he cares to read them, they are all there.
It seems to me the minister is watering down what-

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I am not watering down anything.

-I understood the undertaking to be. 1 thought we
Supply-Defence Production were going to have these contracts filed with the committee. As I understand it, the minister is now saying that when the appropriate officer is before the committee he will give evidence. That is not what I want at all; I want to see the documents. If the minister says they are in the orders in council I am prepared to study the orders in council. If the full information is there, we can get it there and then we will have it. But we do not have it now and I do not think this item should pass until we get it.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I assure my hon. friend that the Department of Defence Production will file with the committee on defence expenditures every document the committee asks for. I believe my hon. friend is a member of that committee. I am not a member, but my parliamentary assistant is. If the committee will ask for any document it will soon be furnished. I do not think my hon. friend, as a member of that committee, can ask me as a minister, who is not a member of the committee, to file documents at any particular time. The committee may not wish to receive them.

This undertaking is looking different to me every minute. First of all I thought it was an undertaking to me or to us who are in the opposition that these would be filed. I now find that they are going to be filed if the committee demands them. The majority of the committee are not in the opposition and they may think that this is a silly request on my part.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I think so; nevertheless I am prepared to file them.

I know the minister often thinks I am silly, but I do the best I can. I want to know just what this undertaking is. It seems to me that its own mother would not know it now. Let us see what the undertaking is. As I understand it, all I have is that if the committee decides to ask for them, then we will see them. That is not good enough. I asked the minister to file these contracts. He said this was not a suitable place to file them, but he would file them with the defence expenditures committee. That is not what is happening now. We are now told that if the defence expenditures committee asks for them we will get them.
I want to go back to the beginning. I asked the minister whether these would be available on Tuesday with the defence expenditures committee. I asked the minister to produce them in the defence expenditures committee and the minister agreed. Now he is substituting something for what I asked.

Table them here.

Supply-Defence Production
That is what I asked.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: They are tabled here. How many times do they have to be tabled? This is absolutely repetitious. Every authority to make a contract, with all the details, has been tabled in this house. If my hon. friend will go to the proper sources he will have what he wants. If the committee of which he is a member wishes to review them the department will furnish them for that purpose, but my friend knows as well as I do that you cannot file documents with a committee unless the committee is willing to accept them.
The minister should not try to get me into trouble by offering to do something that cannot be done; he should not do that just because I am young and innocent.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Those are not the adjectives I would use; just the opposite.

You cannot insult me half as much as my friends over here do. Let us go back again. If the minister says these orders in council have the contracts fully embodied in them, there is no reason whatever why the contracts should not be filed as well and then we will have them.
I am a member of that committee and as far as my memory goes no document that has been asked for by any member of that committee has been refused.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production; Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Not one yet.
Whether my friend is right in saying that no documents have been refused may not be important, but certainly a good many requests have been refused.
That is not the same thing.
I am coming right back to where I was. Will the minister file these with the committee-it was his own suggestion-or will he not? Will he table them here, or will he not?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I will permit the committee to decide what documents they want. If they ask for them, I will give them to the committee. I will not table them in this house again because they have already been tabled.
Then the item does not carry tonight.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
It would not carry tonight anyway.
Item stands.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: topic
Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on Monday we will proceed with the following bills and resolutions: Third reading of Bill No. 242, to amend the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act; Bill No. 194, to amend the Aeronautics Act; Bill No. 289, to amend the Canada-France Income Tax Convention Act, 1951. Then the resolution respecting the Immigration Act and the resolution to amend the Combines Investigation Act. We will then move to go into supply. It has been agreed that we will go into supply without debate, but we would not call any new departments. We would then proceed with the estimates of resources and development and public works.
No defence production?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Oh, you will not let it pass.

speechtext:
At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.

79. Departmental administration and payments to Canadian Commercial Corporation and other corporate agencies for services provided in connection with defence purchasing and production, $7,332,492.
